items.body:
Nairobi, Kenya’s KMRU debuts on Mego with a suite of serene ambient scenes after emerging with Four Tet-like electronica releases in 2019 and recently starring on ‘Alternate African Reality - Electronic, Electroacoustic And Experimental Music From Africa And The Diaspora’

Known as Joseph Kamaru to his pals, KMRU was hailed by RA as one of ’15 East African Artists You Need To Hear’ in 2018 and is a regular performer at Nyege Nyege Festival in Uganda, beside performing at CTM and Gamma Festival. For his Mego release ‘Peel’ it appears he’s been listening to label hero Fennesz, the Austrian experimental guitarist, or Will Long aka Celer, with whom his tracks share a certain, longing melancholy in their long, sighing arrangements of glistening and creaking ambient pads and mournful post-rock/cienmatic elegance. 

“The subtle calming atmosphere within Peel belies the compositional prowess as layers of delicate sounds wrap around each other creating a hybrid new form ambient musics both captivating through it’s textural depth and kaleidoscopic patterns. The track titles lend themselves to the themes and mood set within: Why are you here, Well, Solace, Klang, Insubstantial and the title track. This is a deep heartfelt journey with a new strong voice being expressed through the means of organically presented electronic ambient sounds, one which reveals further layers on repeat listens.”

items.body:
Decades into a career that began at Paris's fabled GRM, Argentinian innovator Beatriz Ferreyra is still worlds ahead, transmuting environmental recordings and snake-like foley rustles into cosmological whispers that ponder the universe's big questions. 

Commissioned by the French state, "Senderos de luz y sombras" (or pathways of light and shadow) is the latest transmission from Beatriz Ferreyra, who composed the half-hour, 16-channel piece between 2016 and 2020. She was inspired by astrophysics (specifically the time before the Big Bang), and the world of the unconscious mind, and dedicates the composition to the memory of sound sculptor Bernard Baschet, electro-acoustic innovator Bernard Parmegiani, and her friend Carlos Pellegrino. 

If you've heard her  GRM releases, or Room40's two essential anthologies ("Echos+" and "Canto+"), then you'll no doubt already be intrigued - that material helped to cement Ferreyra's well-deserved place in the canon, her work speaks for itself. Ferreyra's fathoms-deep tape manipulation experimentation has inspired countless artists, from Keith Fullerton Whitman and Jim O'Rourke to Debit and Valerio Tricoli, and this latest full-length just reminds us how open-minded and freely experimental her compositions can be.

The piece is split into two side-long chunks, both of which tremble with eerie uncertainty. 'Senderos abismales' is gusty and effortlessly psychedelic, using carved-up field recordings to suggest familiarity before sending us wheezing into the cosmos. Ferreyra doesn't need much: the distinct sounds of tyres on wet tarmac, wind whispering in the distance, and distant birdsong are sculpted into a giddy, multidimensional lattice of chiseled sonics and ponderous philosophy. Her confidence is key here, and she never needs to do too much; the negative space is just as important as any chaotic moments, and the tiny breaths of harmony - from icy winds, spectral processing, or something else entirely - sound as if they're provoking life in a vacuum. Comparatively 'Senderos del olvido' is more upbeat, beginning with exploded star sound design that shifts thru a sci-fi spectrum without using any of the usual pneumatic sound effects that have become customary.

Ferreyra is too thoughtful to rest on obvious cultural totems. Her vision of cosmic emptiness is strikingly human; when she voyages into the abstract, her gurgling, digitally-reduced textures only remind us of the soul behind the complex processes. And just as her '70s tape music allowed us to feel an emotional connection to music that was too often lost in academia's back rooms, "Senderos de luz y sombras" reminds us that the same is true of contemporary computer music. If you enjoyed the run of recent Roland Kayn reissues, this one's gonna be absolutely required listening.

items.body:
Sferic/Faitiche emissary Roméo Poirier pairs up with stylistic mentor Jan Jelinek on a sampler's delight, answering Jelinek's romantic 2005 gem 'Collage of Digital Passion' with a montaged mirror image that fizzes with plunderphonic warmth.

Jelinek has been using The Exposures pseudonym since 2003, most notably pillaging micro-samples from numerous R&B records on "Collage Of Digital Passion” issued by Prefuse 73’s Eastern Developments label back in 2005. In his by-now inimitable loop-finding style, that track has become a bit of a low-slung classic, reminding us not only of his iconic productions of the early 2000’s, but also of Anthony Shakir’s iconic ‘Mr. Shakir's Beat Store’ from just a couple of years earlier.

For his “version”, Poirier flips “I hate you!" samples with fanciful, theatrical soundscapes that ooze warmth, capturing the essence of Jelinek's original perfectly.

items.body:
Formally known as Rabbitfoot, 1000 Rabbits survey their first months and years of activity on this brittle six-track EP.

Since they first assembled in Aldeburgh two years back, 1000 Rabbits have tracked from living room to rehearsal space to stage, working through ideas and concepts to come up with a tight selection of experimentally-minded art pop that should appeal to fans of Wet Leg and Black Country New Road. If you've come across the band before, you've probably run into 'Virgin Soil' a featherlight fusion of staccato string plucks, time signature switches and orchestral swells that sits at odds with vocalist River's nonchalant recollections. 'Rubiks Cube' expands the concept a little more, adding a proggy synth low-end and more elaborate drumming, but it's the non singles that convince us that 1000 Rabbits are more than a novelty name. Peep the gossamer 'Bear Hunt', that sounds as if it coulda come from Clarissa Connelly's 'World of Work', or the lengthy, folk-flecked finale 'Spring Cleaning'.

items.body:
The entwined timelines of Bristol, Africa, and Peter Gabriel’s WOMAD festival and Real World label, manifest across eight previously unreleased, early ’80s jams by a mix of West African, Jamaican and Avon-based musicians, at best in the polyrhythmic groovers by Ben Baddoo International, and an unusual sort of proto-trip hop fusion by Bhundu Boys frontman, Biggie Tembo, with Startled Insects, who would go on to key work with Massive Attack and Madonna...

“It’s more than a special moment when you discover music you’ve never heard (of) before or ever knew existed. 1982 was a critical spark for the development of wider (world) musical styles, both in Bristol and the UK at large. The central event from that year was the first WOMAD festival, held in the unlikely surroundings of the agricultural themed Bath and West Showground near Shepton Mallet in Somerset.

One common thread in Bristol to all of these discoveries was the Ekome Dance Company and most notably Artistic Director, Barrington ‘Barry’ Anderson. Barry had also recruited musicians from African countries such as Cameroon and Ghana, from Jamaica and others from the Bristol area. This was to form the Ekome Arts Band which would offer music with either a specific African or Caribbean focus.

This kickstarted a process and practice in the West Country city where musicians brought over from African countries would collaborate with those from the locality. It is those activities - a sound clash and culture clash, producing material of real depth - that constitute the three different combinations, along with one connection originating in London, that make up material on the first The Bristol Meets Africa Music Sound album, released on Bristol Archive Records.”

items.body:
Enigmatic anonymous "dub-kraut" outfit Ferries return with two more spangled sides of helium-voiced Damo Suzuki-worship and copious tape echo. 

We can't tell you who Ferries are, but the band clearly have chops. They appeared out of the aether on last year's 'Eye Flutter' and carry on in much the same vein on 'Eye Wander', making sly cultural references but keeping things mostly buttoned up. It's one of those records that's just balanced on the very precipice of nostalgia, sounding almost like a Can tribute band  - but pulling it back just before it topples into parody. And it's their tightness as an outfit that makes it so easy to chew on; whoever the vocalist is, they're able to soften the band's 'Future Days' worship and conjure surprisingly pop-forward "proper songs" from the Liebezeit drum patterns, dubby basses and troweled-on tape echo. It's nothing you won't have heard before, sure, but it ain't half nicely done.

items.body:
Rattly, stripped-to-the-bone IDM gear that harks back to simpler times, BOT1500's second proper album is simple and elegant, more concerned with the emotional weight of its melodies than the complexity of its beats.

You might remember Shinichi Koboyashi's last BOT1500 album 'Surreal', that appeared back in 2022 on AD93's Lith Dolina sublabel. And since then he's been relentlessly prolific on his Bandcamp, issuing regular single track updates that chart his creative process. But 'The Black Sea' is his first longer set in a while, assembling a handful of tracks that highlight his recent interest in minimalism, emotion and dub production techniques. The familiar monosynth groans and dry, jazzy breaks on 'Abstract Springs' might resemble Squarepusher for a moment, but it's much chillier, sparser gear, with space around each element that softens the impact of the hyperactive edits. And on 'Shadows', that same mood pervades the track even when the beats have been silenced; Koboyashi gives just as much importance to his chiming analog synths, coaxing out fragile melodies that sound as if they've been plucked out of time.

And there's a precision to his programming that's immediately impressive. On 'XB 1', his soft focus glitches and woody hits graze the post-dubstep landscape but subtly reframe it, setting the meticulous rhythms against echoing single note sine hits and melancholy pads. And the track's sequel 'XB 2' is an even harder punch to the gut, with exquisite melodies and knife-edge drums that shuttle us right back to 1996 for a moment, an underground dominated by Clear Records, Spymania and Rephlex.

items.body:
Ambitious but still as dreamy as their earliest gear, Mojave 3's third album snapshots a band in transition.

Nowhere near as glossy as its successors 'Spoon and Rafter' and 'Puzzles Like You', 2000's 'Excuses for Travellers' finalises Neil Halstead and Rachel Goswell's flirtations with country and folk by reining in their ambitions, aiming for reliability rather than experimentation. Sadly, Goswell doesn't get much chance to shine, but when she does appear on 'Bringin' Me Home'  it's a good reminder of how effective her voice is in almost any context. Backed by some synth from none other than Mark Van Hoen, she provides a much-needed palette cleanser and high point that sadly wasn't expanded on.

items.body:
Mojave 3's final album, released in 2006, 'Puzzles Like You' is a slick, sunny break from their reverberating early albums.

Undoubtedly the most controversial album in Rachel Goswell and Neil Halstead's Mojave 3 catalog, 'Puzzles Like You' didn't feel exactly like the end of an era when it appeared, but the start of a new one. By this time in the band's evolution, the traces of Slowdive had completely disappeared - which made it all the more surprising when the band re-formed in 2014, effectively ending Mojave 3 for good.

Going back now though, knowing how everything worked out, it's interesting to hear how Goswell and Halstead were motivated to keep up with a shifting industry, reacting to indie's forward motion by kissing goodbye to shoegaze mere moments before they'd become flavor of the month again.

items.body:
Krautrock’s longhair godfathers flocked to a Berlin lake in 2018, playing rarely heard fan faves such as ‘Why Don’t You Eat Carrots?’, accompanied by the Richardchor Neukolln choir, and captured - crowd noise included - on digital recorder for posterity. Trust they still know how to veer from rocking swag to wild-eyed noise like few others...

“August 4 2018 in the scorching Berlin sunshine, Faust performed a truly stunning and unique set, featuring iconic material rarely, if ever, performed live. What made this so special was hearing such pieces as “Why Don’t You Eat Carrots?” played live, with the small choir perfecting that part of the song. For those lucky enough to have been there, they witnessed a Faust show never seen before, or ever to be repeated.

This CD was recorded on a professional digital recorder (not a phone!!!). It has been lovingly remastered by Amaury Cambuzat, possibly the only person capable of doing so, without compromising the nature of the show. Nothing has been added, so there will be imperfections. It comes packaged in a mini LP gatefold wallet, with a gloss spot varnish.”

items.body:
Custom-built for sunny days, Sofie Birch’s solo Stroom debut melds bossa and psych pops with delicate touches of 4th world ambient jazz and chamber music in a chiffon-layered, naïf dream sequence landing somewhere on the line between Sam Prekop's self-titled alltimer, Antena's Camino Del Sol x Stereolab on the downbeat...

"This album is created over the past years with my brother Alfred. This period has been spiritually transformative for me. it reflects the playfulness and authenticity that comes out of releasing deep traumas and healing wounds. this music comes from a deep place of joy and connection with my brother and with the essense of being a child. being filter free and in contact with the most uncomplicated and loving parts of ourselves, still emphasizing magic and mystery, like childhood does without asking for permission or confirmation.

It took me a while to actually see the music as an interconnected piece. i have been taking in and out material, re mixing, removing, rearranging, re producing and regretting all along the way. but suddenly when we mastered this selection on a cassette tape recorder, the meaning started to reveal itself and drawing threads back in time.

Bivabippalukka is playfulness, intuition, transition and myths. the page of cups. the ideas rising, the energy flowing, flowers, stars and jumping creatures on the verge of dimensions. fortune telling, magic cards, secret caves and things that disappear right in front of you. many talented guests playing with me and my visions on the album.

Bossa nova is the most comforting genre for me. and we need comfort in these times. we need comfort to heal and feel joy to be able to keep dreaming and manifesting - and transmuting the world.

I am not gonna play this music live in the form it appears. i will still continue playing spiritual ambient music. this work is something else. it is pocket of joy, a cup with a fish. it is a step on the journey, like everything else."

items.body:
A trenchant UK steppas dub masterpiece, 1993, mercifully returns to vinyl for the first time in over 30 years. Pure soundsystem tungsten produced by TNT Roots and Winston Dread, with OG copies known to trade for triple figures, making this remastered edition a no brainer.

As regularly deployed by Aba Shanti-I and Iration Steppas sounds - both titans in their field - Earthquake Studio’s ‘Dub Harder Than Steel’ is a definitive lodestone of UK digi-dub; a distinctive mutation of the original JA style, seeded on blighty by descendants of the Windrush generation. The sound’s influence resonates deeply with the roots of so much dance music that we hold close to heart on this island - jungle/D&B, UKG, dubstep, and beyond - leading, over time, this particularly platter to be hailed a true holy grail. 

Cooked up on a relatively basic array of a DK-80 synth, Yamaha keyboard, Casio RZ-1 drum machine, and an Atari 1040 computer running Cubase V2.0, Earthquake Studio’s innovative sorcery is found in the way they spatialise and massage the machines’ frequencies to inimitably mystic, transcendent, propulsive effect. Subs go lower than the Dead Sea and natty melodies ring out like reedy sirens according to a unique democracy of the frequency spectrum that really comes into its own with just amplification. Trust laptop speakers will not suffice; you need a proper rig to get the best out of this one: the bigger, the better.

Echoing the likes of Jah Shaka’s ‘Commandments of Dub’ precedents, but in a digickal style & pattern in step with the times, and even more concentrated to fundamentals, ‘Dub Harder Than Steel’ is as good as it gets for the type of proper gut-rumble, nose-flare, heavy troddin’ pressure whose impact can be heard across UK soundsystem music, especially the sort of stuff practised by Digital, Muslimgauze, DMZ, or Raime.

Don’t sleep!

items.body:
Back on Lolina's Relaxin label, great area turns in three tracks of plugged-in (but endearingly casual) DIY pop that's sure to speak to fans of Smerz, Astrid Sonne and Tirzah.

Like last year's impressive 'Good Coding' album, 'Love' infuses modern home-made pop with tongue-in-cheek humor and impressively deadpan lyrics. "There's doom in the data," she coos listlessly over canned violins and bone dry beats on 'Audiences change but you stay the same". It's a love song that sounds as if it's been copy pasted from a sequence of offhand texts and diary entries and the accompaniment is a canny update of the twee pop formula, replacing a full band with DAW instrumentation and Factory-style basslines. 

'Noises in a row' is another surprising earworm, extended with its trance-y keys and psych-style organ vamps, but it's all about the closing title track, a brittle electro-tinged schoolyard rhyme that's part HTRK, part Heavenly.

Bonkers plunderphonic cut-up of Heiner Goebbels & Alfred Harth’s sampled rendition of 1960’s Revolutionary Pekinese Opera from China, helmed by experimental force of nature Otomo Yoshihide on turntables & guitar.

“With the blessing of OTOMO himself, one of the cornerstones of nineties avant-garde officially returns to vinyl. A melting pot of musicians, sounds, and experimentation, all masterminded by the Deus Ex Machina of Fukushima. These compositions haven’t lost a single shred of their original allure, striking us today with the same raw power and innovative drive of thirty years ago, when they first burst onto the global avant-garde scene.”

items.body:
On Kirk Barley’s definitive solo gem, alternative tunings and a tactile feel for pitching rhythms generate their gentlest and most absorbing work, twinkling amid a microcosm of similar, exploratory productions from Mark Fell & Rian Treanor thru to Aleksi Perälä, Beatrice Dillon, Terry Riley & Jon Hassell.

Building on a decade of work spanning cuts for Brownswood thru to jams with Matthew Herbert and Matt Davies, ‘Arc’ finds Yorkshire-bred artist Barley fully indulge formative passions for microtonal just intonation - as seeded in Terry Riley’s ‘Shri Camel’ - and slippery syncopation to the fullest. Half solo, proper, and half peppered with percussion by regular spar, Matt Davies, it follows his nose for open frontiers of alternative tunings and wonky meter with the blend of low key modesty and prism-pushing tekkerz that have long endeared his work to lovers of lower case experimental music. 

Sweetly balanced between timeless, folk-soul-wise and futurist sensibilities, the half hour suite knits hyaline synths and rippling gamelan metallophonics with clarinet and guitar in lissom, sloshing shapes that effortlessly seduce, rather than demand, the listener’s attention. In particular we are drawn to the bits in duo with Davies, floating sublime ideas in the dreamlike, inverted dub architexture of ‘Ion’, settling on mind like a strangely bucolic Incus work on ’Sundry’, and thru the exquisite, tip-toed rhythms of ‘Ecstatic’, to a trippier, bittersweet type of ante-chamber music on ‘Fret (Hear)’.

He’s also deeply charming when left to his own devices. Ambient opener ‘Billow’ calls to mind the tenderness of Cotton Goods works, and ‘Knead’ chases a certain geist of Irdial or Plaid-esque gamelantronica into the sublime title tune, while ‘Prism’ most beautifully ties all his interests in a melting dream sequence which he caps with the harmonic nightlight glow of ‘Column’.

items.body:
Brixton beatmaker Omari Lyseight parades his mid-Atlantic bonafides on 'Digital', tapping MIKE, Earl Sweatshirt, Niontay and Lerado Khalil as well as locals like Jawnino and Jadasea.

One of the most impressive things about the Surf Gang stable is that it refuses to confine itself to New York City. evilgiane's collective is outward-looking in the best way, reaching across the country and across the pond to make connections between various local sounds that usually get left to chance. Lyseight's no stranger though; he's spent the last few years immersing himself in the US scene, producing for MIKE, Lucki, YL and others while keeping a foot firmly in South London. 'Digital' displays this constant motion, mixing up his production - that seems to have been inspired by everything from Bay Area bounce and vintage trap to grime and UK funky - and providing his collaborators with plenty to work with. 

MIKE, who we last heard from on the 'POMPEII // UTILITY' double album, sounds particularly comfortable slurring from the top of the dome over Lyseight's foggy synths on 'Like or Repost', and his sparring partner Earl Sweatshirt sinks his teeth into a rack of redlined 808 kicks and kinked flutes on 'Square'. 10k's Niontay's also more than comfortable following Winter's brilliant 'Soulja Hate Repellant' with the 8-bit banger 'Gotham City's Finest', maybe the mixtape's most replayable track. But Lyseight's closer collaborators put in the work, too: Jadasea cuts through distortion and interference on early highlight 'Detonate the Fuse' and Jawnino returns to Surf Gang with the anthemic 'drugsintheparty'.

One of the year's standout releases - and winner of the 2005 Mercury Music Prize.

'I Am A Bird Now', the second full-length from this extraordinary New York artist and her cohorts, features contributions from both peers (Rufus Wainwright, Devendra Banhardt) and heroes (Lou Reed, Boy George). Their involvement reflects both their admiration for Hegarty, and her unique place in the contemporary arts community. "Everyone's presence on the record shows them at their most unique, making a special contribution that is specific to them," says Hegarty.

items.body:
Peak Oil boss Brian Foote and scene veteran Paul Dickow (aka Strategy) work at the intersection of classic electronic music, dub techno, city pop and bleep techno on 'High Cube', plowing decades of experience into a taut set of highly atmospheric and jazzwize downtempo grooves. RIYL Move D, Lifted, The Detroit Escalator Co., Purelink.

Longtime pals Dickow and Foote have worked together in various outfits for decades, but somehow never recorded as a duo until now. For ‘High Cube’ they set themselves strict parameters, allowing themselves five bits of gear and one hour to create each track, leaning into the constraints to yield maximum creative energy. 

The album's spontaneous flow is powered by rickety beatbox loops, emotive synth sequences and levitational pads that point to a classic, jazzwize era of electronic music and especially the Detroit-influenced diamonds Dave Moufang produced as Move D and as part of Reagenz, Studio Pankow and Conjoint in the mid 1990’s. It’s all elevated, atmospheric and uplifting, spiralling synth lines dissolved into the airiest production style - an almost naive retro-futurism that feels pure and almost hopeful three decades on from the OG’s.

Peep the free-flowing blips and throbbing bassline on 'Underwater Welder' that the duo season with distorted FM growls and cycling, slo-mo beats, or the weightless, mytho-tropical mood they evoke with just a few elements on the hypnotic 'A Dragon's Treasure is its Soul'.

Maybe they do make them like they used to, after all.

items.body:
Jazzy 1977 rework of a traditional Japanese wedding song, backed with Visible Cloaks’ weightless ambient electronic remix

The 1977 version was conceived by Jazz man Jun Arasaki and his group Nine Sheep, and executed in one take (this recording) on five sanshin, four winds, piano, bass, percussion and drums for a TV broadcast. It’s somehow solemn yet joyous in a slow and stately way, with lyrics describing how “beautiful buds unfold”.

Fourth World inhabitants and dreamers Visible Cloaks remix ‘Kajyadhi Fu Bushi’ in their own image, resulting a diaphanous, gauzy swell of harmonised synth chorales infiltrated by playful ghosts in the machine and weft with elusive traces of the original vocal to sound like a Google deep dream reverie of the real thing.

Recombinant raver Low End Activist warps dark garage, grime and jungle with bugged-out braindance-jazz flourishes on a definitive solo salvo for his private folio.

Written and released circa his debut LP ‘Hostile Utopia’ (2022), the five tracks of ‘Low End Activism 004’ pursue a more peculiar, rugged yet atmospheric type of Rephlexian geist loosely related to the LP’s themes of nostalgia for lost futures. 

Flint-tuff dark garage/grime of Slimzee’s ilk flexes taut tendons and Burial-esque pads in ‘Curtian Twitcher’, beside echoes of AFX’s detuned strings woven with breakbeat hardcore swerve on ‘Fractal’, subtly betraying the artist’s links with Avon and West Country styles. 

Centrepiece ‘Wow’ marries DJ Narrows-esque dark garage pressure with debonair keys on a daring highlight of the EP, next to the slippery early grime-meets-electronica recoil of ‘Clocks Ticking’ and masterful finishing move of eldritch dark garage like Burial and BoC on a rude one.

items.body:
Retrospective of elegant rare groove and folk-pop from Phnom Penh’s golden age of sound in the 1960s and 1970s.

"In those vibrant years, the city pulsed with music: rock bands, crooners, and traditional ensembles blended East and West, shaping a uniquely Cambodian pop that shimmered with hope and modernity. Amid this flourishing scene, So Savoeun’s voice stood out—silken yet powerful, intimate yet expansive, carrying with it the promise of a new era. This collection brings together rare and long-unheard recordings, including luminous duets with legendary contemporaries Meas Saman, Lek Savath, and Sinn Sisamouth.

Each track is more than just a song—it is a fragment of memory, a preserved echo of nights when Phnom Penh’s dance halls and radios overflowed with rhythm and possibility. In her own words, hearing these songs resurface is like opening a long-buried chest of jewels, hidden beneath the dust of history and now gleaming again after half a century. Her voice, once thought lost to time, reemerges like the cicada whose chant reverberates endlessly through the forest—an eternal call that bridges silence and remembrance. Her music is more than nostalgia; it is testament and rebirth. It continues to resonate, not only with those who lived through that golden era, but with new generations discovering its beauty for the first time. Through this release, the past breathes again—tender, luminous, and unforgettably alive."

items.body:
Mercurial electro-techno steppas and rollers by LA’s Maude Vôs, moonlighting from Delusional Records onto fresh label, Gravity Pleasure.

The six tracks of ‘Medicinal Properties’ pull from Vôs’ extramusical cues of queer culture, travels in Ireland, Iceland and Montreal, and their natural worlds, for an elegantly mesmerising take on breakbeat techno modernism. Cinematic sound design and whirring rhythmic programming wraps up in calm yet urgent forms, ranging from the needlepoint step and hyaline synth pads of ‘Orr Kore’ and the EP’s title tune, thru the clipped sort of post-dubstep gait to ‘Sap Sanctuary’, and halfstep cyberdub lean of ‘Jasmine Seson’, to windswept electrostep tekkerz in ‘Endless Fliuch’, and dBridge-esque widescreen Autonomic sublime of ‘Swimming Saracnade’.

items.body:
Bit of a special one from John T. Gast’s 5 Gate Temple, finding anomalous wildcard St Agnis with a set of classical guitar improvisations under the Victoria Mingot alias - all enchantingly loose-limbed lowercase strums and murmurs tipped for fans of Loren Connors, Graham Lambkin, Virginia Astley, Vincent Gallo, Klein.

‘God Spill’ runs like a diary of broken sleep, taking things to their quietest, most ruminative depths. The dozen pieces are defined by plaintive melodic structuring for classical guitar, voice and pedals, on what sounds like dictaphone recordings that imbue everything with an eerie ferric intimacy. And those vocals are pretty special when they do appear, like a flickering filament in the aether of ‘i saw the sign’, recalling Mary Maddox off Mike Ratledge’s ‘Riddles of the Sphinx’, floating, Virginia Astley-like, on the frayed Lambkin-esque strum of ‘in plentitude of the harvest’, or more textural in the mournful raga meditation ‘om dhyana’.

The exquisitely discreet balance of un-showy yet transfixing instrumental economy is magnified by an un-moored sense of time and place and what the label call “soft rage” -  fully revealing itself with repeat listens.

Special stuff.

items.body:
Vaporwave catalyst Spencer Clark (The Skaters) responds to the paintings of Belgium-based Croat artist Vedran Kopljar with some of his lushest, worm-holing, inter-dimensional synth trips.

Some 15 years since the first instalment of The Spectacle of Light Abduction, Clark takes cues from Kopljar’s vividly surrealistic windows of invention to dive headlong into polychromatic alleys of the mind. A sense of ceremonial ritual emerges in passage from the herded rhythms and aeolian winds of ‘Abyssfields’ into the high plains drift evoked by ‘Abomination Plateaus’, adapting prevailing winds of new age ambient and Troma-esque synth gunk to put a proper breeze behind one’s noumenal sails and leave lots to the imagination. Trust it’s not the corny signposted pish that vaporwave has become, but a visionary, world-building immersion in Clark’s magnificent inner world, a place familiar yet strangely displaced from normality, where the synths exhale pure DMT-like fractals and tickle atavistic reaches of the amygdala.

items.body:
Future modal jazz dub, heard thru a Y2K lens by legendary blowers Pharaoh Sanders & Graham Haynes, and diffused in Bill Laswell’s illbient dub style & pattern. A slept-on, cross-generational ace sure to pique interest FFO Jon Hassell to Talvin Singh, Lászlo Hortobágyi to Material.

Cooked up in NYC’s jazz crucible in 2003 as a duo of Sanders & Haynes - now re-mantled as a Sanders x Laswell session for its first vinyl cut - ‘With a Heartbeat’ speaks to the rich confluence of deeply rooted, forward-thinking jazz with ambient dub that tilted from the late C.20th into this century. Centred on the human heartbeat, it unfurls at a rested systolic throb in two landscaped-scale works which bookend deeper dives into Indian raga and tabla actions, the latter of which may find favour on open-minded ‘floors, due to its effortless, toes-off-the-ground levity. But essentially, it’s idealised for floating at home or road tripping on the astral highway.

Bill Laswell’s name at the top signifies his integral input, but with no discount to Graham Hayne’s cornet, beautifully knit in warm, rising air with his peer, pioneering tenor sax player Pharaoh Sanders, who brings a half century of chops with Coltrane, Sharrock, and myriad others, to the plate. Quite simply it’s a lush listen from front to back, opening from heartical subbass pulse into 17 mins of dusted illbient dub with a cool reserve on ‘Across Time’, and shoring up in almost big beat 4th world fusion scapes reminding of the eL-Hortobãgyi Hortator album with ‘Gamaka’.

Yet we’re most partial to the midsection, where Sanders & Haynes colour the luxuriant space and rolling ballast with a wider range of brass and woodwind in the dewy raga of ‘Morning Tala’, and Trilok Gurtu’s undulating and spicy tabla and scatting vox evoke an aerial game of hashed-out kabaddi in ‘Alankara’.

items.body:
Lauded London composer Blumberg preceded work on ‘The Brutalist’ and ‘The Testament of Ann Lee’ OSTs with this skeletal, yet quietly intense, live solo showcase.

‘GUT (Live at the ICA 23.05.23)’ frames Blumberg and his devices - vocals, bass harmonica, diatonic harmonica, Steinberger ebass, electronic drums, synthesiser - at his rawest and most inventive. Shards of song and percussion pierce negative space coloured with drone and physical convulsions, captured with canny mic placement to best present his full use of the stage. The results call to mind everyone from Frank Tovey’s performance art to the more operatic urges of Anohni or John Bence, and even latter Scott Walker in his embrace of freeness, stark lacunæ, and edging discipline.

items.body:
Autechre's reissue engine reaches their outstanding 2008 album, featuring definitive moments of their near 40 year (and ongoing) run.

‘Quaristice’ is Rob Brown and Sean Booth’s 9th studio album as Autechre, conceived some 20 years up-to-the-hilt in their thing, and depicting the duo emerging into a sort of hybrid live x studio jam style that’s distinguished much of their work thus far. However archänlèy, it’s still not even the best version - that honour is reserved to the 2.5hr digital-only ‘Quaristice.Quadrange.ep.ae’ brimming with extended versions, including an hour long mix of ‘Perlance subrange 6-36’ and deadly 10’ mix of ‘Tkakanren’ - but suffice it to say we’re made up to see this one in the wild on vinyl, at least.

The follow-up to a pivotal standout, 2004’s ‘Untilted’ (also reissued this year), ‘Quaristice’ really felt like a future upgrade to the system on its release in 2008. Completely unconcerned with prevailing or emerging trends of dubstep or UKF at the time, it sees the duo follow their noses for hardware/ software jams into the proper mutant body music, milling limbs to the meanest 112BPM electro swag in the twin-rotor electro hip hop gnash of ‘Tankakern’, and utterly wrecking the senses in the blizzard dynamic of ‘Fol3’, or manipulating sinew with deviant liquid B-Boy tekkerz on ’90101-5l-l’ - each of which feature in even better versions on the 2nd disc (and frankly better yet in their alternative extensions of the digi-only version). 

There are flashes of the melodic and harmonically curious Autechre we all know and love in opener ‘Altibzz’ (their love note to the magic of Altrincham), the aerated strings of ‘Theswere’, and almost Lynchian noir of ‘Notwo’, yet the whole thing feels to trigger muscle memories and flashbacks to club physicality, as felt in the corresponding live show at Pure in Manchester at the time. The mad thing is, as judged from recent live show, they still sound as rudely uncompromising and propulsive now, 17 years later, perhaps more than ever

items.body:
Mojave 3's dreamy sophomore album, originally released in 1998, returns to 4AD with a brand new lick of paint from its Abbey Road remaster.

By the time 'Out of Tune' was release, shoegaze felt like a distant memory. Even Britpop's dominant influence had started to fade by this stage: Pulp released 'This Is Hardcore' and post-rock bubbled into a rolling boil, Slowdive had become an afterthought. But Mojave 3 were surprisingly popular, their impeccably written alt-country snatching fans from Tindersticks and Hope Sandoval. Sadly, 'Out of Tune' wasn't quite as ineffably beautiful as their debut, marked by clarity as Halstead moved further away from the Slowdive sound and ditched the reverb completely, but it's still worth a look.  

'Some Kinda Angel' is an engaging duet that highlights the power of their swelled lineup (with Simon Rowe joining on electric guitar and Alan Forrester on organ and piano). And 'Yer Feet' is between Radiohead and Leonard Cohen - a minimal slow burner that shows just how good Halstead was at writing simple, effective songs.

items.body:
Nearly three decades since it was created, The Durutti Column's "lost" fourth album is finally issued - with Factory Benelux catalogue number 36, and all.

According to legend, the original album was scheduled for release on Factory's Belgian subsidiary but an executive decision from Tony Wilson shelved it in favour of 1984's 'Without Mercy'. 

Some tracks have appeared on Crepuscule's beautifully curated compilations over the years, but ultimately this is a real missing gem from the early Factory era: all skeletal drums, sparse daubs of synth and violin, Vini's iconoclastic virtuosity, and just the feel of the pieces, all transporting us to some high-ceilinged apartment in Brussels or Didsbury with the hum of hash in the air.

Tipped FFO Manchester old-timers, Balearic types and dream pop lovers...

items.body:
Emotional Response presents the first of 2 EPs by Laura Sparrow aka LNS, the Calgary raised, Berlin based producer and DJ with 8 acid-tinged cuts that are equally expansive and inspiring, personal and inventive.

Sotofett spar and Tresor resident, Laura Sparrow aka LNS explores more atmospheric strains of her club sound, touching on Chicago deep house and Tin Man-esque acid, thru to flighty braindance jungle and electro

For 10 years LNS has built a staunch rep via countless sets at Treso’s Globus and dozens of drops for her LNS label and Sotofett’s Wania. She now takes the opportunity to spread wings on off-peak styles, following fine-wrought 303 lines into the chirruping shuffle of ‘Sweet Acid’, the Larry Heard-alike ‘Micro Acid’, and brisk Mike Dred-type flex of ‘Cosmacid’, to an electro-acid gem ‘Acid Rated’ comparable with classic Analords. She really knows how to make her machines purr, as on the dream motion of ‘Alive Acid’, while her ‘Blue Acid’ could also be mistaken for a Rephlex classic.

Back in the game after his ace ‘Poly’ LP helped reboot Ostgut Ton, Efdemin plays true to his minimal techno form on four driving workouts with Dekmantel.

Armed with a refreshed, rugged palette and hunger for tuffer techno, Phillip Sollmann marks some 30 years of fuelling the ‘floor with the ‘Mirror Phase EP’, which escalates in increasingly hard-edged turns from the title tune’s harmonic Berlin-Via-Detroit techno to sludgier acid techno teeming with strange voices in ‘FS1R’, into full Motor City-style flight, a la ‘Landcruising’-era Carl Craig, on ‘Unity Grain’, and the brisk, tweaked-out trot of ’Slip’, which builds to a glorious posh trance peak.

items.body:
Arriving in 2003, 'Spoon and Rafter' features some of Mojave 3's best-loved songs, Beatles-influenced wall of sound productions that bolstered the songs with theremin, glockenspiel and melodica.

The folk and country elements were beginning to wear on Neil Halstead and Rachel Goswell as they trundled into the 2000s. Their fourth album felt like a shift, but a welcome one; after a few years of boxy, shoegaze-inspired folk and alt-country, the expansiveness of 'Spoon and Rafter' made sense, especially in the wake of bands like Neutral Milk Hotel and Olivia Tremor Control. It's still recognisably Mojave 3, but repackaged for the lucrative US market - hardly surprising then that the record's big tracks, 'Billoddity' and opener 'Bluebird of Happiness' were both synced to kingmaking TV show 'The O.C.'.

items.body:
Moß Garten's "Sekvensstyrd 1981–1986" via Anna Logue Records.

"40 years after its creation, MOß GARTEN – Sekvensstyrd 1981–1986 arrives as a compelling double vinyl LP, diving deep into the early Swedish DIY electronic scene. Inspired by pioneers such as Kraftwerk, Cabaret Voltaire, John Foxx, and The Human League, Mikael Isaksson developed a distinct sound situated between minimal electronics, industrial, synth wave, and experimental sound art. At its core was the sequencer: pulsing, programmed structures forming the backbone of dense, often hypnotic compositions.

Working initially with his cousin Jan or friend Thomas and later evolving into a largely one-man project, recordings were made on cassette tapes and in improvised studios—often under time pressure, frequently recorded and mixed within just a few hours. These very limitations gave the tracks their raw and immediate character. Pieces like “Moderna Kvinnor,” “Soon Soon,” “Ensam,” and “Music From The Border” exemplify the uncompromising, sequence-driven (“sekvensstyrd”) approach that defined this era.

Using an arsenal of analog synthesizers, early sequencers, and drum machines, the project created music that feels at once cold, mechanical, and deeply emotional. Sekvenssytrd 1981–1986 is more than a collection of archival recordings—it is a vivid document of a time when electronic music was conceived as a radical and deeply personal form of expression.

Mastered by Martin Bowes. Graphic design by Steve Lippert."

items.body:
Antony has long been a purveyor of a darker brand of cabaret, but last year he exhibited an unexpected turn collaborating with premier league kosmische type Dan Lopatin aka Oneohtrix Point Never and noise/ambient Godfather Christian Fennesz. This willingness to push his sound into more peculiar places can instantly be heard on ‘Swanlights’, not least from the submerged drones of the title track. Antony’s vocals sound more pained and cavernous than ever, and rather than the more traditional clean piano, his voice is accompanied by a shimmering, distorted guitar and doomy plucked bass. The result is a track that revels in a Lynchian quality we rarely hear; ‘Swanlights’ captures the upended pop referentialism of Lynch’s America and places us right in the darkness, surrounded by light. The real draw is going to be Lopatin’s inspired rework of this track however; taking the already squiffy vocal, Lopatin underpins soaring synth strings, expertly chopped-out arpeggios and his signature wavering leads. The result is both nausea inducing and utterly captivating, showing a new side to Lopatin’s production and re-affirming the fact that sometimes remixes can be just so lush. Huge recommendation.

items.body:
Takahide Higuchi searches for light in the darkness on their follow-up to 2023's 'uchigawa tankentai' EP, a surprisingly personal collection of mutant children's songs and playground rhymes that Higuchi subverts with chipmunked voices, cartoonish samples, Mark Fell-like FM synths and rhythms inspired by Brazilian funk, footwork and ghetto house.

Reflecting the stress and strain of the modern interconnected world, Higuchi controls the chaos on 'HIKARIGASASHIKOMU', appearing straight out of the gate with a chorus of corrupted voices that are pitched into alien screams, paired with shrill digital stabs and ketmized FX. It's disorienting stuff, far more eccentric than the MIDI-jazz-footwork echoes that characterized 2021's 'Yasuragi Land'. Here, Higuchi appears to be turning their distant childhood memories into demonic ghost chants and hypnogogic club inversions: nursery rhymes that have been chopped to shreds and spliced with hiccuping beats. 

'Omoi' is like SND making footwork, while lead single 'Hard Reclining' is a seemingly mismatched fusion of folk-y vocal chants, vintage R&B guitars licks and flimsy city pop drums. Then on 'Horomiro', after being blasted by squelchy acid sequences, we're hit with a barrage of cartoonish samples: woody hits, repurposed gliding squares, transformer scratches and chaotic vocals. It's almost too much, standing in stark contrast to Higuchi's relatively spare early work. But thematically it's on point; Higuchi wants us to live in his world for a moment or two, experiencing his internal world so we can get a better handle on his psychedelic sound.

items.body:
One for haunted dancehalls: Severin Black serves Riddim Chango’s Parallel Line a trio of moon-booted, anti-G dub and heavy troddin’ steppas FFO TNT Roots, Element, G Version III...

Aberystwyth-via-Berlin producer, Severin Black ov The Fat White Family and Archaic Vaults, trades in ruggedest pressure on both sides of his debut with Japan’s mutant dub torch carriers. Up top, he leavens a worm-charming subbass quake with flyaway flutes x vapourised dub chords to tip-toed steppas effect on ‘Brandy’, next to the more severe pressure inversion of ‘Yarmouth’, packing cantankerous levels of bass grunt and sandpapered percussion to ruff up any dance. The B-side is counterweighted with ‘Cautious Dub’, a 9 minute trip driven by gunky digi pulse and tonsured choral synth voices mashing down babylon, reserving a flicker of hope in the 2nd half that soon gets extinguished.

items.body:
Eglo co-founder & Rinse FM resident Alex Nut continues to come into his own as a producer with deep cuts of beatdown soul and broken beat sagely nodding in the direction of Dego, Waajeed, Theo Parrish.

Nut is feeling the funk three different ways on his 3rd solo EP issued in the past 12 months. His DJ-honed club instincts and feel for timeless soul feed forward into the lo-slung shimmy of ‘Bright’, glazing a Detroit-style house strut with harmonised and cut-up vocal motifs bathed in warmest keys, before lacing it with a skudgy acid line for later in the night on its ‘Re-FreQ’ mix. The heat keeps knees up, hips swivelling, on a classic Y2K West London broken beat flex mutual to his and Floating Points’ tastes, whereas ‘Duck Duck’ really dials it down to with a bed ways glyde in its velvet-clad bass and dreamily vapourised chords.

items.body:
For new initiates and avant-garde fiends alike, this Xenakis collection renders a breathtaking survey of works by the radical composer, theorist, architect and engineer, spanning the period 1956-1974 and featuring some of the greatest works of the 20th century, including the awe-inspiring sonic architecture of ‘Persepolis’.

Inarguably one of the most important composers to blend electronic process and classical orchestration, Greek-French artist Iannis Xenakis made an indelible impression on the 20th century with his staggeringly complex feats of musical engineering. Regularly cited as an influence by composers ranging from Florian Hecker thru Autechre and Reinhold Friedl, Xenakis’s polymath pursuits in hybridising music, architecture and mathematics generated a bewildering array of sounds and structures which have rarely, if ever, been bettered in terms of their sheer scope, scale and technical ingenuity.

It’s possible to break down Xenakis’ approach to composition, and its results, as an extension of his experiences in armed combat, fighting for Greece’s left wing liberationists against the German army and later the British during WWII, with the latter leaving him blinded in one eye. He would eventually leave Greece in 1947 after graduating university with a degree in civil engineering, and before he could be conscripted into the Greek army, who didn’t look favourably on left wing sympathisers. Moving from Greece to Paris left him with a sense of guilt at betraying his friends, and a sense that “I had to do something important to regain the right to live. It wasn’t just a question of music - it was something much more significant.” 

That significant something turned out to be a mind-blowing, multi-disciplinary oeuvre practically unprecedented in the history of music, architecture and art; a radical synthesis of ideas which embraced new technology and abstraction as a means to realise and create a new world in the aftermath of WWII. Like the Italian futurists before him, Xenakis would draw on the chaotic soundfield of war, and combined with a strong knowledge of experimental classical music and a special nous of maths, Xenakis’ subsequent studies with Olivier Messiaen and work with Parisian architect Le Corbusier would prompt him to composing groundbreaking new music during the 1950s.

This 2CD contains works from that era, stretching right back to the pranging clangour and jet-like eruptions of Achorripsis [1956-57], an early example of his stochastic style of composition, thru the dizzying, chronic dynamics of Syrmos [1959], and to some of the earliest work composed by a computer, the 7090 IBM, in ST/48(St/48-1,240162).

But it’s Xenakis’ ’60s/‘70s work where his genius is mst evident, from the breathtaking scope of Polytope De Montréal [1967] - written for four orchestras in the same space in the French Pavilion at Expo ’67 - to the gobsmacking dimensions of his seminal Persépolis [1971], which was realised for the Shah of Iran, plus the frankly terrifying, computerised wormhole of Polytope De Cluny [1972-74].

We can’t reasonably describe this set as anything other than indispensable for fans of electronic music from its inception to the modern day.

items.body:
A decade since debuting as Ndagga Rhythm Force, Mark Ernestus’ incredible band draw on 100’s of hours studio and live practice for a staggering new suite of Senegalese x Berlin-styled mbalax steppers that prove, where needed, why they’re one of the best to do it right now. Absolutely exemplary, transcendent music for those that know.

Back at the start of the 2010s dub techno pioneer Mark Ernestus was spending a lot of time in Senegal, immersing in styles and patterns that historically underlined the reggae and dub musics he would heavily reference in his pivotal records made as Maurizio/Basic Channel/Rhythm & Sound, as co-produced with Moritz Von Oswald during the ‘90s and into the ’00s. 

In the process of researching and getting down to the roots of his passions, Ernestus encountered some of Senegal’s top tier musicians and recorded the Jeri-Jeri ensemble, revolving vocalist Mbene Diatta Seck and sabar drummer Bada Seck, and generating in 2013 the ‘800% Ndagga’ CD and its ’Ndagga Versions’ sibling, which better showcased Ernestus’ famed dub tekkerz inseparably woven into Senegalese music and the roots of myriad Afro-diasporic sounds.

That unit would morph into Ndagga Rhythm Force, producing an LP and trio of 12”s in 2015-2016 that set them on course to become one of the most impressive African bands on the contemporary gig circuit, throwing down live sets known to effortlessly go over 2 hours and propel so many legs and minds to new shapes and feels - trust they slay every time and should be top of all must-see lists.

With ‘Khadim’ Ndagga ditch their guitars and recalibrate a more lissom trio of voice and acoustic instruments bound with Ernestus’ Prophet 5 synth - the same model he’s relied upon since the Basic Channel days - on four extended songs that allow more light, space and emotion into a signature, rolling sound, centre-staging Mbene Seck’s husky diva croon over Bada Seck and Serigne Mamoune Seck’s dual, polymetric percussion, and judiciously juggled with Ernestus’ anti-gravity basses and plangent dub chord syncopation. 

In traditionally open-ended frameworks the quartet take all the time needed to stretch out and wrap heads into the tapestries of their storytelling grooves. A newfound atmospheric pressure and presence emerges in procession from the location recordings that fringe ‘Lamp Fall’ and its ode to a local mosque, reverberating in acres of implied space set by the ricocheting sabar drums and near-infrasonic subs, thru to the devotional depths of ’Nimzat’, rippling with thunderous chords and doleful ache. 

At its core are the LP’s most impressive parts; ‘Dieuw Bakhul’ uncoils a spellbinding Wolof tale of treachery to the rafters amid tempestuous chords that writhe stereo-wide with red-lining bite whilst drums knot sinuous, serpentine, to be resolved in the breathtaking 13’ steppers’ flight of ‘Khadim’, which lyrically hails Islam’s role in guiding Senegal to postcolonial times, spiritually meditates on bluest minor key riffs, and physically elevates bodies with aerodynamic finesse and hypnotic chronics kin to the best reggae and its offshoots. 

Deadly, soul and hoof gripping tunes. Do not miss!

items.body:
Another transmission from Naarm's fertile underground, 'The Key to the World' is the third offering (and first outside of Australia) from wyrd pop eccentric Sam Perry and features a cover of Lana Del Rey's 'Mariner's Apartment Complex'.

There's a DIY character to this one that feels totally intentional. The album was recorded in home studios peppered across the world: one in Belgrade, one in Christchurch and one at home in Melbourne. And it's ramshackle without being too disjointed, rolling from short, baroque interludes to bona-fide electro pop bangers at the drop of the hat. Even in a single track, Perry's able to burn down the borders between his influences, casting a glance to Prefab Sprout and Syd Barrett on the ace 'Life's A Party' before it dissolves into a chaos of tape-fluxed euphoria. 'Lake of Ice' comes off like a lost cue from one of Werner Herzog's '80s features and then there's that Lana Del Rey cover, of course.

items.body:
Expanded double vinyl edition of Sex and Death, the 11th studio album by lauded Factory Records ensemble The Durutti Column.  Originally released in 1994 on CD, the album has now been re-mastered with 5 bonus tracks and appears on vinyl for the first time in a coloured vinyl edition.

"The writing and recording of Sex and Death closed an uncertain period for Vini Reilly and the group following the collapse of Factory Records in 1992. Factory founder Tony Wilson remained in post as manager of the band, but Sex and Death would be their last album with producer Stephen Street, famed for his work with Morrissey, The Smiths and Blur.

Writer and master guitarist Vini Reilly remained philosophical. “People say the Durutti Column is this or that. I don’t care, so long as we make good music. There’s screaming feedback on some tracks, heavy metal guitar, Spanish picking. It’s not just this ethereal trip. Don’t listen to the form, never listen to the form. Listen to the content.”

Stand-out tracks include Anthony (dedicated to Wilson), The Rest of My Life, and Believe In Me. Guest musicians include viola player John Metcalfe, vocalist Ruth-Ann Boyle (later to form hitmakers Olive with Tim Kellett), programmer Martin Jackson (Magazine, Swing Out Sister) and bassist Peter Hook, then on furlough from New Order post-Republic.

All 5 bonus tracks are previously unreleased, having been retrieved from a long-lost DAT tape located in Tony Wilson’s personal archive. All tracks on the album have been newly re-mastered in 2020 by Peter Beckmann and Technology Works."

items.body:
Green Gartside and co’s addictively sugary turning point album crops up for a masterclass in blue-eyed soul styles.

Upon its release in 1985, ‘Cupid & Psyche 85’ marked a radical leap for the once squat dwelling communists from new wave dreamers to chart-worthy pop pucker. Prior to this record they had markedly political and philosophical leanings set to a mix of almost folksy whims, disco and reggae lite, as found on a handful of Rough Trade releases, but with ‘Cupid & Psyche 85’ they mounted a sly assault on the charts, drawing on Green Gartside’s love of Aretha Franklin’s aching soul for a far more polished sound that would parallel the likes of Prefab Sprout’s entry to the US billboard charts.

In many ways its not hard to draw lines between Gartside and the Sprout’s Paddy McAloon; both are reclusive genius types who saw the other side of the pop machine and disliked it, and both made some of the ‘80s greatest power moves, as Scritti Politti did with the likes of ‘Absolute,’ which now uncannily reminds us of trotting around Co-Op during early lockdown (it was on their in-store radio A-list), and the natty funk of ‘Wood Beez,’ their seminal prayer for Aretha Franklin, which is coincidentally co-produced by Arif Mardin.

items.body:
Mika Vainio & Ilpo Väisänen’s first ever release as Panasonic, originally issued in 1994 as the "Panasonic EP", a while before they were forced by the electronic goods coroporation of the same name to drop the A...

A real slice of history right here, presenting longer and harder versions of a cut that appeared in a shorter form on Mika’s Ø album ‘Metri’, co-credited to him and Ilpo, and here going longer and doubled up with another duo battering ram, ‘Murtaja’. Both tunes sound very much of their time, when European techno was forged tougher to demand, paralleling movements of harder Chicago house and Detroit warehouse techno.

In Panasonic’s case, the results were typically ascetic, mostly bleached of discernible melody beyond rhythmelodic cadence, and locked, bloody-minded, to icy tattoos that reflected their origins in Finnish warehouse parties, and would pin them on the international techno and electronic music maps. Trust that ‘Muuntaja’ still leaves welts from its distorted kicks, and contains subs primed to quake foundations, whilst the B-side is ideal for gnashing rave punks and bass drum fetishists.

items.body:
Antony & the Johnsons: 'Cut the World' is a collection of live symphonic performances of songs from the band's 4 full length albums.

Hegarty kicks things off with the album’s only exclusive composition, the title track ‘Cut Hands’, and sets the pace with this richly orchestrated epic. The whole album was recorded with the Danish National Chamber Orchestra, so hearing fleshed out versions of some of the standout gems of her career sounds like Hegarty is rewarding us just for being fans. These versions are so different from the originals that they almost stand up as new works, and the care and attention put into ‘Cut World’ makes it worth the asking price alone. Recommended.

items.body:
Since the release and subsequent ubiquity of her breakthrough album, I Am A Bird Now, Antony Hegarty seems to have appeared on an endless list of other people's records, featuring heavily on the Hercules & Love Affair long-player, and making notable appearances on Bjork's Volta album.

On certain collaborations Hegarty's voice has seemed a tad out of place (My Robot Friend's 'Rapture' being a particularly strange one), and that's surely because her voice is now so inextricably tethered to the aching piano arrangements of pieces like 'Hope There's Someone' and 'Cripple And The Starfish' that it's strange to hear her tremulous falsetto put to any other use. The Crying Light is an expansion of - rather than a departure from - established Johnsons territory: not content to languish in the sweet, lyrical melancholy established by prior works, Antony embraces a sound that marries desperately lovely orchestral arrangements with abstract, dissonant timbres - embracing a juxtaposition between exquisite ornature and dark awkwardness. This manifests itself on 'One Dove' via a number of surreal anharmonic interjections from an array of unlikely instruments (what sounds like shakuhachi, dulcimer and possibly even some fragments of electronics), while 'Another World' combines sparsely phrased, plaintive chord changes with soaring discordant tones in the background, making for a pained counterpoint to Antony's supremely elegant vocal. The Crying Light might lack the celebrity guest spots of I Am A Bird Now (there's no Lou Reed or Rufus Wainwright on here), but musically, lyrically and in terms of overall vision it's a considerable step forwards.

items.body:
Death Is Not The End return to the soul-stir sound of deep south Sacred Harp Singers in 1993 - although it could feasibly be any time since the advent of portable tape recording - in the blessed company of the Union Grove Baptist Church, Ozark, Alabama. Feels just right in this humidity…

The Wiregrass Singers' Dewey Williams began learning the shape-note tradition in his childhood. He studied under Judge Jackson, who authored the landmark 1934 hymnbook The Colored Sacred Harp. In 1971, Williams formally organized The Wiregrass Sacred Harp Singers to preserve the music full-time. This unified troupe began touring nationally and leading workshops, which ultimately launched them onto stages at the Smithsonian and Newport folk festivals up until Williams' passing in 1995 when the group disbanded. The African-American Sacred Harp tradition in the Wiregrass region has steeply declined since the start of the 21st century, due to an aging generation of singers, and today it is largely sustained through archival preservation and occasional multi-book singing meetups.

This raw recording, made at the Union Grove Baptist Church, Ozark in mid-April 1993 finds the group singing from B. F. White’s The Sacred Harp (1844), which together with his brother-in-law William Walker’s Southern Harmony (1835) formed the musical backbone of generations of Southern music and Southern musical styles.

items.body:
Recombinant raver Low End Activist properly came into his own on this ’21 slice of inch-tight jungle saluting legendary inspirations from 4Hero to Photek, Source Direct, Digital and On Remand - and now newly pressed up to vinyl.

After minting the project in 2017 and cultivating grime mutations ft. Trim and Flowdan, Berlin’s Low End Activist more fully indulged passions for formative jungle touchstones on ‘Engineers Origin’ - the 1st plate under his eponymous label, part of a family with his prolific Sneaker Social Club. 

Entering a field of lockdown-spurred jungle emulators, LAE brought a real finesse to his sharply stylized mid ‘90s homages that elevates his work above the crowd. On the title tune he summons proper darkside spectres with poised balance of sci-fi atmosfear and technicality certain to keep toes off the ground, before ‘Look Up’ snaps into the tightest steppers motion with flinty drums and exquisite use of a screeching string sample from On Remand, and ‘Probability 1’ seals the deal with a sonorous subbass pressure cadged from Dead Prez, alloyed to depth-charged breaks.

Cold and deadly!

items.body:
Ostgut Ton’s freshest recruits trade in effortlessly rolling bleep techno and moodier meat motors primed to be played in the big house.

Along with the likes of Quelza and Inox Traxx, Berlin-based Justine Perry & Paula Kossi lend an injection of new blood to Berghain’s label revival. Their ‘Paired Works’ oscillate energies between Perry’s effervescent levity and Koski’s rolling momentum, with the latter at best on the stealth build of ‘Beyond the Line’ and finely poised, teasing pressure of ‘Opaline’, while Kossi best impresses with the concentrated, urgent canter of ‘Maeve’, with its plucky bassline, plus the dub chord-riding ‘Adnexa’, and Fadi Mohem-esque elegance of ‘Held in Place’.

items.body:
Sweden’s rich jazz heritage feeds into Mariam Wallentin’s smoky groovers with the 10-piece big band Vestnorsk Jazzensemble, unwinding from the tango of ‘Blanket Dance’ and a Portishead-esque ‘Basel’ to bare their teeth on the rugged ‘Love Is Fire’ and Susanna Wallumrød-alike, cinematic ballad ‘Wide’, that hints at Mariam’s background singing the theme tune of HBO series ‘Raised by Wolves’.

"The album originates from Wallentin’s stay in Basel in the spring of 2023. There, with the Rhine as a constant sonic backdrop, a series of diary notes began to take shape. She brought these fragments to Bergen, where she met the West Norwegian Jazz Ensemble. Initially intended as rehearsals, the sessions took place in a studio — Mariam realized the opportunity had to be seized. She out the crumpled notes from Basel she had in her bag, now almost distilled into lyrical fragments, small clouds of chords, memories and impressions. Over the course of just two days in the studio, they shaped and explored these ideas together into something collective, through openness, presence, deep listening, and intuitive interplay. The result is an album consisting of seven original pieces and a rare cover, moving between the tender and the insistent, the airy and the electrified. The music can whisper like grass or surge like a spring flood — where red symbolizes tenderness, blue melancholy, and everything revolves around the longing that spring awakens within us.

The West Norwegian Jazz Ensemble is known for its ever-changing line-ups and close collaborations with selected composers. The project with Wallentin arose from an invitation by the ensemble and developed further through concerts and a strong sense of collective interplay. The recording took place over two days at Duper Studio in Bergen and captures a moment of musical presence where ideas and expression emerge in real time. The ensemble consists of a wide range of musicians who together create a rich and dynamic soundscape: from harp textures shimmering like flowing water, to percussion inspired by the sounds of nature, and a core rhythm section that drives the music forward with both weight and lightness. Spring Flood is an album about movement — in nature, in the body, and in relationships. It explores the fleeting and the enduring, the individual and the collective, and music’s ability to open spaces for both reflection and presence."

With witty lyrics and an abundance of catchy songs, New Wave Graveyard is a thrilling statement from an exciting new artist."

items.body:
Berlin’s influential EBM-techno figure plays to his taut variation within meat-motor themes: from sinuous purism to bleep attack and darkwave guile

A key cog in the modern EBM machine, Phase Fatale brings signature aerodynamic tension to each cut, holding tight to seething arps shot thru with a frisson of sci-fi romance on ‘Immobile Symmetry’, and twanging glute with the needlepoint 16th note arps of ‘Guts’, whereas ‘Blue Rose’ twirls bittersweet bleeps for the gnashers and, best of all, ‘Off Desire’ resets the formula with fine lines of Sandwell District-esque synths and a darkwave bassline bound to do the damage in the right settings.

items.body:
A spiritual session of seminal nyabinghi grounation from Dadawah circa 1974, perhaps the most mind-expanding, important spiritual dub reissue we've heard this last couple of decades and inarguably a template of sorts for the whole burial mix aesthetic. It doesn't get much more influential, or spiritual, than this one.

Dadawah were led by Ras Michael, guiding a traditional set up of nyabinghi (ceremonial Rasta drums), bass, guitar, brass and Piano organ in four extended excursions over sublime, psychedelic terrain in a mode that sounds uncannily like a precursor to Rhythm & Sound's 'Making History' from decades later.

As with much of the best material from the era, much of the magic was elicited and embellished in post production, with Lloyd Charmers and Federal engineer George Raymond apparently staying up all night after the session to mix the recording, imbuing the tracks with a dazed, wide-open and echoing personal space.

Keeping the standards impeccably high, the album was lovingly restored at Abbey Road and comes housed in heavy stock, hand assembled card sleeves, looking every bit the classic that it is.

Aside to private dubplates, ’Snippet Sounds’ is the French multi-instrumentalist’s first record, proper; a carousel of gently psychoactive and subtle skews on convention that chimes with soundsystema nd dub outliers such as Sheriff Lindo or Tapes, or the rest of the of the... more
items.body:
Class vinyl debut of Lee ‘Scratch’ Perry’s live band bass player, Slim Levy, trading in charmingly dare-to-differ cosmic dub sorcery on an ideal home for this type of lark - Disrupt’s indomitable Jahtari.

Aside to private dubplates, ’Snippet Sounds’ is the French multi-instrumentalist’s first record, proper; a carousel of gently psychoactive and subtle skews on convention that chimes with soundsystema nd dub outliers such as Sheriff Lindo or Tapes, or the rest of the of the Jahtari kru, for that matter. 

Taking equal cues from his former bandleader (he played on Perry’s last tour), and The Beach Boys’ ‘Pet Sounds’, the set reels to 14 succinct and DJ-ready parts, dancing between toytronic vignettes and more fully formed knees-ups that echo the strange, innovative spectres of ‘70s Black Ark output via more lo-fi tekkerz.

To play favourites, we advise checking for the plucky, air-step skank of ‘Chalaladub’, the rickety ‘Chim Cherie’ vintage vibe of ‘Characteristics’ and ‘Train Train’, or perfectly sozzled drunken master style of ‘The Evil Cowboy Condor’, thru the early digickal bubbler ‘Wake Up John’. But ultimately we reckon it’s best taken in one go, where the tidgier bits come into their own in an album context.

'Insalar' means 'humankind', 'kime ne', 'so what', 'what of it'. Villalobos rends the 23-minute original nearly three times the length in a slowly blooming 3D soundsphere. more

The concert contains songs from the first three Antony And The Johnsons full length albums - ‘Antony And The Johnsons’, ‘I Am A Bird Now’ and ‘The Crying Light’ - as performed by an ensemble of musicians including Maxim Moston, Rob Moose, Julia Kent, Parker Kindred, Jeff Langston and Thomas Bartlett. Plus two rare Antony And The Johnsons studio recordings from that period.

items.body:
The most memorable moment of  Music, Fashion, Film  comes during its first track and lead single, "Rock Music." Musing that she thinks the dance floor is now dead,  Charli xcx  turned heads by ditching the party girl persona that had fuelled the culture upending  Brat . As an act of bear-baiting it worked, but in truth, the proclamation was to be taken no more seriously than James Murphy’s turn-of-the-century observation that the kids were selling their guitars to buy turntables, both absurd theses that ignore the immortality of these institutions. Determined to challenge the standards of legacy and fame, her eighth studio album and second of 2026 offers a set of buzzy guitar pop that retains her charm without leaning on euphoria as a crutch. 

The pace has changed, the personnel hasn't:  Music, Fashion, Film  was produced entirely by PC Music founder A.G. Cook and label regular Finn Keane, two longtime collaborators who are crucial within the Charli-Industrial Complex. The glimmering quality of their pop production is still present, like on the shining synth melodies of "Camera" or the deep warbling sub-bass on "Card Declined," but it's now locked behind a steady flow of Pixies-esque guitar crunch and drum machine automation.

The rough edges of the instrumentation feel authentic, perhaps even a little unvarnished. Cook and Keane's band  Thy Slaughter  has previously approached this style of rock music via electronic, but the atmosphere feels akin to the laid back ambience of French soft pop duo  Air , injected with alternative icon  Steve Albini 's sonic forthrightness.

Whether it's the little vocal chops on "Rock Music" or the watery delay that gives "Camera" its urgency, the production duo are able to find a lockstep synchronicity with Charli's droll existential musings about throwing it all away, the vanity of legacy and generally ruining everything about her life. Overall, there's a charm to Charli's songwriting, making it relatable to even the greatest cynics. 

"Wink Wink" brims with whimsical synth melodies and a catchy hook that starkly contrast the observational verses about aging out of the fast life ("I used to jump on trampolines with no underwear on / and now I basically just wear trousers"). Flexing similar muscle to  Brat  and  how i'm feeling now  staples like "Girl, so confusing" and "anthems," the experienced songwriter is able to wrest an uncharacteristically exciting pop tune from the depths of her anxieties and insecurities. 

In spite of a short runtime,  Music, Fashion, Film  leaves you craving more. Take "Yeah," a hilariously bare track even for the songwriter's standards. It's burdened by an aimlessness found in the first song a teenage garage pop punk band would write, thanks to its repetitive power chords and shallow lyric pool. For a popstar at her level, the urge to rip it up and start again is fresh, but not as fresh as it once was—you can only ride a self-destructive streak so far. 

By the time "Magic Metal Montana" rolls around, a clunky but sweet tribute to A.G. Cook, the diary-style lyricism wears thin. Though she's often been confrontational, her writing can feel particularly unfiltered on songs like "I'm Afraid," where she lays her emotions so bare that it can feel borderline juvenile, as anxieties and insecurities can often seem. "Sympathy Is A Knife" took a similar route to a better outcome. What these songs do achieve, however, is to humanise an artist whose persona became so supersized that it risked crushing the person under it. You come away with a sense that Charli needed to make this record for herself, as much as anyone else. 

Towards the end of  Music, Fashion, Film , cult favorite director David Cronenberg offers some words of advice: "As I was lying there on the sidewalk, I did not think about art, at all," the  Videodrome  director muses on "No One Lasts Forever." "It can turn out that, yes, some artists have created art that has really survived thousands of years…but experientially, they are dead." 

If this is Charli's way of shirking immortality and strategically wrapping her arms around  impermanence, then it worked. Little resembles a new pop classic, however. Will that be enough to satiate the new fans who, post- Brat , look to her as an oracle? Perhaps not. But it feels almost innovative for an artist at the peak of their success to ignore the rat race and create something unfamiliar. By presenting a more intimate set of material than the crossover hits that launched her to global It Girl in 2024, Charli appears to have faced down the deathly industry cogs that have chewed up and spit out so many before her.

items.body:
KATSEYE have returned with a fierce new single. The global girl group unveiled 'Animal', a flirtatious pop anthem that explores the contrast between the polished personas people present to the world and the uninhibited versions of themselves behind closed doors.

Co-written by Ed Sheeran and produced by Omer Fedi and Blake Slatkin, the track pairs magnetic pop production with playful lyricism, transforming themes of secrecy, attraction, and impulse into an empowering statement. 'Animal' serves as the latest preview of WILD, the group's third EP, which is set for release on 14 August via HYBE x Geffen Records.

The accompanying music video leans into the song's duality, unfolding across observation rooms, mirrored realities, and shifting identities. Directed by Cody Critcheloe — who also helmed the group's 'Gnarly' and 'Touch' visuals — the cinematic clip features dynamic choreography, surreal imagery, and a cameo from Academy Award-nominated actress Demi Moore.

'Animal' follows KATSEYE's first single of the WILD era, 'PINKY UP', which the group debuted live during their Coachella performance. Fans can also look forward to KATSEYE: WILD HEARTS, a limited theatrical release beginning 12 August, ahead of the group's sold-out KATSEYE: THE WILDWORLD arena tour, which kicks off on 1 September.

items.body:
JENNIE is ushering in a softer side of her artistry with the release of her new single, 'Less than a Lover', out now via ODDATELIER/Columbia Records.

Serving as an ode to summer, the alternative-pop track captures the lingering emotions of a relationship that exists somewhere between friendship and romance. Written by JENNIE herself, 'Less than a Lover' pairs lo-fi guitar textures and vintage electric keyboards with intimate vocals as she reflects on the excitement and uncertainty of an undefined connection.

The accompanying music video, based on a story by JENNIE, follows the BLACKPINK star as she steps into another version of herself while filming a short movie with friends. As the fictional romance unfolds on set, the lines between performance and reality begin to blur, reshaping the dynamic between the characters.

The singer first previewed 'Less than a Lover' during her headline performance at Governors Ball in June, before bringing the track to festival audiences at Mad Cool, Open'er and Roskilde. Next, she is set to headline Lollapalooza Chicago before making her debut at Summer Sonic in Japan.

As one of pop's defining global stars, JENNIE continues to expand her artistic range through music, performance and creative storytelling. With 'Less than a Lover', she leans into a more understated sonic palette while exploring the complexities of connections that don't fit neatly into labels.

Glow Festival by Prudential wrapped up its fifth and largest edition after welcoming 100,000 visitors to Sentosa over ten days, with live performances from Jason Derulo, HYUKOH, Alessia Cara and more taking centre stage alongside the festival's wellness programming.

Held from 10 to 19 July at the Palawan Green Festival Grounds, the festival combined more than 70 wellness sessions across eight immersive zones with a three-night concert series that drew crowds long after sunset. While Glow has established itself as a wellness destination, this year's music line-up reinforced its growing appeal as a lifestyle festival where live entertainment and wellbeing go hand in hand.

Friday saw Jason Derulo open the weekend with an energetic headline set at the Cupola Stage, before Korean indie favourites HYUKOH took over on Saturday with a performance that drew a devoted audience. The festival closed on Sunday with Alessia Cara, whose soulful set provided a fitting finale to the three-day music programme.

Beyond the headline concerts, festivalgoers spent their days moving between beachfront yoga, fitness classes, wellness workshops and social spaces spread across the grounds. Standout moments included sold-out sessions led by Joe Wicks, packed classes at the Flow Studios, and bustling activity across Mind Oasis, Makers Meadow and Recharge Bay, while Glow Commons served as a gathering point for food, drinks and downtime between activities.

The 2026 edition also marked a milestone for the festival, with Exceed Sports & Entertainment, Prudential Singapore, Sentosa Development Corporation and the Singapore Tourism Board formalising a strategic partnership aimed at strengthening Glow's position as a long-term global wellness event. The festival further expanded its footprint across Sentosa through activations at several hospitality venues, extending the experience beyond the main festival grounds.

Glow Festival by Prudential attracted 100,000 visitors across its ten-day run, underscoring Singapore's ambitions to grow wellness tourism while demonstrating the increasing role that live music plays in shaping the festival experience.
