items.body: Some records ask to be heard; Philippe Petit’s Lightning Field 01. Constraint asks to be observed, documenting the unpredictable conversation between composer, electricity, and machine at the heart of modular synthesis. Fragments of a larger ongoing investigation Modulisme Session 144. Lightning Field 01. Constraint by Philippe Petit   Modular synthesis releases occupy a deeply specific and persistently misunderstood territory within experimental electronic music—a territory that operates by entirely different rules than those governing conventional recorded sound. These aren’t listening experiences in the expected sense. They’re dispatches. Evidence gathered from the interior of a process most listeners will never witness directly. A conversation conducted between a composer and a system that has its own grammar, its own tolerance for deviation, its own appetite for accident. The best of them carry no trace of manufacture. They feel discovered rather than designed, unearthed from the space between human decision and machine response. At its most essential, the modular release functions less like composition and more like field recording, the distinction being that the field here is electrical, the landscape assembled from patch cables, voltage gradients, and the irreducible uncertainty that lives in the gap between what a composer instructs and what a system chooses to return. Modulisme—the platform born in July 2019 out of Marseille, described as a media documenting left-field modular synthesis, has been building this archive since its inception, reaching session 144 here. The platform operates like a library rather than a label, curating exclusive one-hour sessions from composers working with modular systems across the full range of the form, from academic electroacoustic tradition through to experimental improvisation and everything in between. By session 144, the catalog represents over a thousand exclusive works and a genuine document of where modular synthesis composition stands in the mid-2020s. The artist behind Modulisme is Philippe Petit himself—a Marseille-born composer, DJ, label operator, and self-described “musical travel agent” who has been releasing work since 2000 across labels including Sub Rosa, Monotype, Home Normal, Staubgold, and his own BiP_HOp imprint, which from 2000 to 2010 advocated left-field electronica before eventually becoming Modulisme. He studied electroacoustic music at the CNRR Conservatory, specializing in multi-channeled diffusion and modular synthesis, working with Buchla System 200, Serge 73/75, and a modified EMS Synthi A. His catalog includes collaborations with Lydia Lunch, Edward Ka-Spel, Eugene S. Robinson, and a genuinely vast network of experimental musicians accumulated over decades of restless cross-genre activity. He describes himself not as a composer but as someone who transmigrates source material, an apt description for an artist whose work has always been about the movement between forms rather than the forms themselves. Electricity itself as the subject rather than a medium :: Lightning Field 01. Constraint is the first volume of a new series in which Petit imposes a specific limitation on himself: no acoustic instruments, no vocals, no field recordings. The usual escape routes he describes reaching for in composition—a piano frame, a prepared guitar, voices, found sounds, are deliberately removed. What remains is his Buchla and Serge systems working in isolation, and the results of letting those systems define the boundaries of what’s possible. The title is precise, this is a volume about the founding decision, the acceptance of voluntary limitation, and what that limitation reveals. It’s the same constraint logic that has driven the most interesting experimental music for decades, from Alvin Lucier‘s single-premise compositions to the Oulipo literary movement’s rule-based writing. What happens when you remove the familiar? What surfaces in the space left behind? What surfaces here is a series of works that treat electricity itself as the subject rather than a medium. Petit describes the modular as a miniature weather system whose internal architecture has been laid bare, not an instrument but a machine for intimate storms. That’s not marketing language. It’s an accurate description of how Buchla and Serge systems behave in the hands of someone who understands their particular logic. Unlike Eurorack, which tends toward precision and control, the Buchla and Serge traditions lean toward instability, drift, and the productive unpredictability of analog voltage. A patch on a Buchla system creates relationships between modules that interact and evolve in ways that can’t be fully predicted in advance. The composer sets conditions rather than issuing instructions. What emerges from those conditions is the work. The tracks themselves are labeled in iterations: “Field 04,” “Field 05,” “Field 06,” and so on, through to “Field 15.” Each one is a short burst of electronic bubbles and modular clicks, some containing feedback, others carrying rhythm. They function less as tracks in the conventional sense and more as specimens, individual electrical events captured and named sequentially rather than titled descriptively. That naming convention is itself a statement about what these pieces are. They’re not songs. They’re not compositions in the way that word is usually understood. They’re fragments of a larger ongoing investigation, numbered because they occurred in an order, not because they need to be experienced in one. This recalls the classic modular sessions of the 1970s and 80s, the early Moog explorations of Wendy Carlos, whose Switched-On Bach (1968) introduced the synthesizer to mainstream audiences but whose later works like Sonic Seasonings (1972) pushed into more abstract, atmospheric territory. Klaus Schulze‘s extended Berlin School synthesizer pieces, Tangerine Dream‘s Phaedra and Rubycon, Morton Subotnick‘s Silver Apples of the Moon (1967)—the first electronic work commissioned by a record label, and the musique concrète lineage running through Pierre Henry and Bernard Parmegiani at INA/GRM in Paris all share the same fundamental question Petit is asking here: what does electricity sound like when you stop trying to make it sound like something else? The longest track in the batch is “Field 06,” running at 11:08, and it’s the most melodic of the bunch. It opens with a sequence arp cycling through different tones, rhythms going off-tone and on again, speeds shifting, different oscillators being introduced and withdrawn. More than any other piece here it plays on the melodic and rhythmic side of modular synthesis—the arp becoming a kind of unstable melody, never quite resolving, always pointing somewhere it doesn’t arrive. Much of what’s played throughout the series sits in distortions and rhythms rather than conventional melodic structure, which is consistent with Petit‘s stated intention to let the systems generate the conditions rather than imposing a compositional outcome on top of them. This is not for the casual listener. That needs to be stated plainly. You won’t find structural familiarity here, no verse-chorus logic, no emotional arc that announces itself. These are pieces, not tracks, electrical specimens, experiments in what a Buchla and Serge system will produce when given a set of conditions and allowed to follow its own logic. This is Session 144, and the fact that it’s Petit‘s own session rather than a guest is significant. He built this platform to document the modular synthesis community and has spent years giving that platform to others. Turning the session on himself, and specifically doing so under a constraint he describes as deliberate, as a way of denying himself the usual escape routes, suggests this isn’t a casual exercise. Lightning Field is announced as a series, meaning this first volume of constraint is the beginning of something longer and more sustained. Not obsessively themed, but genuinely exploratory, each volume investigating the same territory from a different angle, the synthesizer as an active field through which forces circulate rather than a machine that produces predetermined outcomes. For an artist who has spent over two decades documenting what other people do with electricity and cables and voltage, this is Petit finally turning the recording equipment on himself and letting his own storm be captured. The sound is no longer manufactured. It is, as he writes, captured. Guided. Transmuted. Whether that transmutation continues to reveal new territory across future Lightning Field volumes is the question worth watching. Session 144 makes a compelling case that it will. Modulisme Session 144. Lightning Field 01. Constraint is available on Modulisme. [Bandcamp] Modulisme Session 144. Lightning Field 01. items.body: The finest quality of Ladybug 1 comes from its ability to treat dub as an art of emotional memory. Each return of the theme seems to erase something and make it more vivid at the same time. In the leaner versions, rhythm becomes a heavy step through smoke, reverbs widen like liquid metal, silences speak with the same intensity as the impacts. Vanishing is the core and the fate of the whole EP Ladybug 1 by The Bug / Dis Fig   With Ladybug 1 EP, Kevin Richard Martin opens the Ladybug series on Pressure through a work of emotional precision. Each chapter will bring a different female voice into his bass universe, and the first presence is Dis Fig, Felicia Chen, already a crucial companion on In Blue (Hyperdub). The memory of that album returns like a call from the dark, and here the step shifts, the air grows warmer, the pulse slows, the matter turns more bodily. The Bug has shaped, across decades, a language immediately his own, born from dub, dancehall, industrial music, spectral hip hop, sound system devotion and lab fever. Chen comes from another fire, formed through noise culture, club practice, wounded vocality and physical performance. Together they find a zone where song becomes atmospheric pressure, and dub moves from genre into inner weather. Vanishing is the core and the fate of the whole EP. Around the main piece, versions, dubs and deeper immersions expand the same emotional event, as Martin opens the body of the music and reveals nerves, vapor, rhythmic apparatus, magnetic blood. The choice moves beyond the simple idea of a remix set and takes on an almost cinematic form: one ghost seen from different angles, one trauma changing density at every pass. The bass carries the weight of a horizon drawing near, pushing from below, bending the light. The percussion advances slowly, with the authority of a machine that knows the measure of pain. Around it, ambient trails, dub vapors, shoegaze reflections and exhausted sensuality gather into music that feels vast, physical, tender in its devastation. It is dub for the end of love, soul for immense systems, electronics speaking to the body before thought. A series debut with the force of something necessary: a handful of tracks, a single emotional center, a depth that grows with every listen. ~Mirco Salvadori Dis Fig’s singing is the point where this mass receives a face. Her voice descends along the lines of sound, melts into the kick, then rises again like a private confession caught by an apparatus far too powerful. The lyrics, written by Chen, seem to follow disappearance after a romantic rupture: the loss of the loved body, the numbness after impact, desire continuing to send signals after contact has faded. The word Vanishing becomes gesture, phenomenon, progressive erasure, almost a way of naming the fading of the self inside the echo of another. Chen sings with feverish grace, close to secular prayer and stripped soul, letting fragility, narcotic sweetness, muted resentment and burning lucidity pass through. Her presence turns the brutality of the low end into feeling, gives the machine a human breath, carries the wound to the center of the system. The finest quality of Ladybug 1 comes from its ability to treat dub as an art of emotional memory. Each return of the theme seems to erase something and make it more vivid at the same time. In the leaner versions, rhythm becomes a heavy step through smoke, reverbs widen like liquid metal, silences speak with the same intensity as the impacts. Martin’s hand knows the tradition of the mixing desk as creative instrument, the lesson of Scientist, the daring of On U Sound, the hypnotic depth of Basic Channel, the mutant melancholy of King Midas Sound. Here those lines enter a new tale, more feverish and sentimental, where sound system culture meets a broken ballad, lover’s rock is projected into a digital night, and Massive Attack appears as a distant memory filtered through exhausted subwoofers. Ladybug 1 chooses concentration. Each impact carries weight, each halo has narrative function, each sonic ghost guides listening toward a feeling of separation that becomes a mental landscape. ~Mirco Salvadori The strength of the brief format lies in its visionary economy. Five passages, a single title changing skin, a progression shaped through subtraction and fever, with the sound seeming to grow larger as ornament falls away. Martin sculpts low air with the patience of a craftsman and the fury of an engineer of controlled collapse; Chen cuts a melodic line across the surface of the magma, curving, trembling, touching silence, then rising again with an almost soul like grace. In a moment when much contemporary music confuses intensity with accumulation, Ladybug 1 chooses concentration. Each impact carries weight, each halo has narrative function, each sonic ghost guides listening toward a feeling of separation that becomes a mental landscape. Ladybug 1 therefore works as a miniature manifesto. It introduces a future series and says plenty about the present of The Bug: the urgency to keep collaborating, to offer his architecture of pressure to voices able to carry risk, desire and biography. For Dis Fig, this return feels like another change of state: from the floating presence of In Blue to a dominant emotional figure, able to bend Martin’s matter toward an abstract blues for saturated times. The music moves slowly, sensually, menacingly, with a beauty born from compression more than explosion. It is dub for the end of love, soul for immense systems, electronics speaking to the body before thought. A series debut with the force of something necessary: a handful of tracks, a single emotional center, a depth that grows with every listen. Ladybug 1 is available on Pressure. items.body: “Qué Loquera”, roughly “What Madness”, is a merengue-driven satire of a planet cooking itself, and of the lovesick singer going down with it. As the world falls apart, Nene del Solar reaches for aguapacheo, his word for wet-kissing on the dancefloor, as the way to carry the grief of man-made catastrophe. The song runs deconstructed Caribbean rhythms, digital synthesisers and chanted onomatopoeia into salsa tumbaos rewired for the dancefloor. It takes the dance straight through the madness of its title, and its AI-generated video turns the tool on itself, a direct hit at artificial intelligence, tech-bros and the way digital life burns through the planet, made by Fabián Mosele and Ali Bardavid. That mix of homemade tropical machines and end-of-the-world dread puts the track in the frame of Caribbean futurism: speculative art that faces down climate collapse and the plunder of the Global South from the region’s own rhythms and beliefs, keeping the machines and dropping the worship of them. The single opens Donde Hay Calor, the debut album from Nene del Solar, released on 17 July through In-Correcto, the Bogotá collective and label that has spent a decade gathering the city’s cumbia, rap, folk and electronic outliers.   Behind the alias is Icaro Lopez de Mesa Moyano, a Colombian sound-media artist who builds the motorised percussion he plays and calls it Los Robots del Ritmo. He works between Bogotá and Bremen, where he is a doctoral candidate, with eight years of traditional Latin American music training behind him, an industrial design degree from Colombia’s National University and a digital media masters from Germany. His projects have played Rock Al Parque at home and SXSW in Texas. Stream “Qué Loquera” HERE and pick up your copy of Donde Hay Calor following THIS LINK The post Daily Discovery: Nene del Solar – Qué Loquera appeared first on Rhythm Passport.

items.body: Review by alainPP — 1. "Can I Tell You" is the opening track from this unique violin-led band?a gritty, rhythmic rock number sitting somewhere between classic and symphonic rock; a fresh experience delivering explosive rock energy.2. "Bringing It Back" kicks off with boogie-woogie piano; the violin and Robbie's vocals drive an energetic, swirling groove. A new sound is born here?one that's hard to pin down to specific influences because it feels entirely original.3. "Lonely Wind" features piano and vocals, with Steve sharing lead duties; note Phil's delicate touch and Kerry's warm keyboards on this killer slow ballad.4. "Belexes" arrives with high-energy keyboards engaging in a musical duel. The melody flows like glowing embers tumbling down a slope; the organ is on fire?fittingly so?and the backing vocals are in full swing. Rich, sporting his signature headband, delivers a sharp, high-pitched guitar solo, cementing the band's trademark blend of keyboards, guitar, and violin. The track heats up further with a final drum solo that sets the listener's ears ablaze.5. "Journey From Mariabronn" is the first of three epic-length tracks; with its violin variations and piano melody, I detect a nod to Supertramp. The song bears a progressive stamp reminiscent of Queen, while the keyboards evoke Yes?heavy stuff! Dave's bass anchors everything and drives the momentum; in short, a magnificent piece of prog rock.6. "The Pilgrimage" returns to a blend of pop, rock, folk, and boogie with a touch of Southern rock flair?thanks to the violin and backing vocals?though it's a bit too brief to truly hook the listener.7. "Apercu" offers a more substantial experience, opening with a spirited energy that leads into verses shared by the two frontmen. The violin ushers in an instrumental section with clear folk undertones, infusing the music with a festive spirit?a fantastic glimpse into their fusion of rock and symphonic styles. The finale takes on an elegiac tone, introduced by a solemn violin before shifting into heavy?or rather hard?rock, driven by the sheer power of the drums and guitar; this intensity carries over into the next track:8. "Death Of Mother Nature Suite," a true grand finale for this distinctive debut album. Here, heavy rock weightiness blends with a melancholic violin. The song navigates shifting harmonic textures, balancing tender sensitivity with the fiery power of the chorus?where the backing vocals truly shine. The guitar solo serves as an immediate reminder that Kansas is a band of the highest caliber. It was undoubtedly a stunning achievement for the genre of folk-infused heavy rock.

items.body: Review by Circuito_Prog — With Pestkr�nikene, Jordsj� celebrates its tenth anniversary without relying on easy nostalgia. Even though the album is built from material written between 2020 and 2025, the Norwegian duo gives it a strong identity and a cohesive concept centered on war, the fall of ancient kingdoms, religious fanaticism, and rebuilding after devastation. Rather than feeling like a collection of leftovers, it stands as one of the band's most cohesive releases.Musically, Jordsj� reinforces the sound that has made them one of the leading names in modern Scandinavian progressive rock. The analog warmth of the production, the prominent use of flute, vintage keyboards, and the balance between pastoral passages and heavier moments create a distinctly Nordic atmosphere. You'll hear echoes of Jethro Tull, Wobbler, �nglag�rd, and even touches of Gentle Giant or Anekdoten, but the band never loses its own identity.One of the album's greatest strengths is how much it accomplishes in just 35 minutes. In a genre often dominated by sprawling epics, Jordsj� opts for compact compositions, most of them between three and five minutes long, keeping the album moving at a steady pace without ever feeling overstuffed. That brevity occasionally makes a few ideas seem to end a little too soon, but it also makes Pestkr�nikene an engaging listen that rewards repeated plays with its intricate details.The guest appearances by Jon A. Henriksen, Andreas Prestmo, and Lars Fredrik Fr�islie add plenty of depth without overshadowing the creative partnership of H�kon Oftung and Kristian Fr�land. Each musician brings something unique to the record, while the production maintains the organic, handcrafted feel that sets it apart from many contemporary releases.Pestkr�nikene doesn't reinvent progressive rock, but it proves there's still plenty of room to expand its boundaries while staying rooted in tradition. It's an album filled with rich atmospheres, memorable melodies, and carefully crafted arrangements that further establishes Jordsj� as one of the most consistent bands in today's European progressive rock scene. It may not reach the grand scale of some of the genre's biggest landmarks, but its authenticity, balance, and genuine love for classic progressive rock make it one of the most worthwhile releases of 2026. items.body: Review by alainPP — Hawkestrel is Alan Davey releasing this 17th opus, distilling the energy of his diverse body of work. Tracks spanning space rock, prog, psych, jazz, and metal, featuring guest artists and original band members. A collection of sensational Hawkwind covers alongside reworkings of songs by Led Zeppelin, the Beach Boys, and Cream."Hall of the Mountain Grill"?featuring piano and flute?is a 1974 track where I find myself desperately searching for Grieg's influence. It is a dark cover, enhanced by Simon's brooding violin. "Brainstorm" channels a Murkey Red vibe?a wild, stoner-punk-psych hybrid blending thick synth, violin, and sax into an apoplectic maelstrom. "Rainbow Demon," an Uriah Heep cover, delivers the organ and riffs of an era before "hard rock" even had a name; Mick's shimmering guitar evokes a vintage feel that invites a nostalgic trip back in time. "Sunshine of Your Love" resurrects Cream's raw, unadorned sound?Ginger's drumming and that vibrant riff flirting with gritty, snarling rock. "Children of the Sun" transports us back to 1971; a heavy riff meets fiery violin, creating a driving track that surfs on psychedelic clouds. Del lets his synth spiral wildly?a touch of Hawkwind meets Ozric Tentacles. "Subterraneans" features vocals reminiscent of Bowie's Robert-era style and a reverberating atmosphere?proto-space-rock "fudge" ahead of its time. Notes swirl, soaking the track in the nascent vibe of early space rock; it ends with an airplane-style outro."Black Dog" features female vocals and Keith's keyboards bursting joyfully out of the solar system?a rhythmic psychedelic cover. "Starcruiser" stands out for its intro?just the way I like it?with Michael's distinctive voice driving a frenetic psych-rock track filled with swirling, wind-like synth sounds. "The Greenfly and The Rose" sees Michael continuing the set, accompanied by a medieval-sounding organ. The drift continues?a pre-emptive stutter of cold wave, pompous art-rock, and Southern rock?floating through cottony limbo. "The Cairene Purse" unfolds over a *Flash Gordon*-esque synth line, a narrative interlude transporting the listener elsewhere to explore a story born of the artist's imagination. "Good Vibrations" is revisited through a psychedelic lens, evoking the latent atmosphere of a parallel universe?as if the Beach Boys had truly conceived the track as a prog-psych-rock testament in the vein of Hawkwind.

items.body: Review by BrufordFreak — A Dutch blues-rock jam band who aspired to Kosmische-style jazz-rock music and, in fact, notably were successful at creating their own particular kind of jazz-rock music while coming from Traffic- and The Who-like blues-rock perspectives.1. "Saras Ritt Durch Schwarzwald" (6:23) impressive Who-like Rock approaching Hawkwind-like Prog or Krautrock. I love Johannes Pappert's Arabian/Indian-styled sax play in the fourth and fifth minute's "interlude." The singing (in Dutch) is like a cross between CAN and early Ozzie. (8.75/10)2. "M.C. Escher" (6:14) the organ-base to the first minute of this one makes it feel like URIAH HEEP but then Johannes' sax enters, taking the wind out of the heavy rock vibe. At the end of the second minute the music totally changes (though still using the same instrumental palette): driving rock drums and bass with long-sustained organ chords. A reliance on a set "heavy metal" guitar chord progression is also reminiscent of bands like Heep, Sabbath, Deep Purple, and Nektar. A brief "normal" voiced lyric in the middle is interesting for its educational attempt. (8.6667/10)3. "Kraan Arabia" (9:45) another droning near-"heavy metal" song that is so quintessentially Krautrock is most notable for the way it exploits Johannes' Arabian sounding and melodic sensibilities on his saxophone. There are a couple sound effects switches on the sax and a few windows for Peter Wolbrandt's rhythm guitar and lead guitar to step into the spotlight. And, damn! Hellmut Hattler is a solid and yet fluid bass player. Note the flange effect placed upon the mics recording Jan Fride's cymbals. The laughter and "smoke-break" breakdown in the eighth minute is rather FOCUS- and CAN-like but it also enables Hellmut the chance to solo a bit (not as good of a soloist as rhythmatist) as well as Jan to show off his conga and supplemental percussion instrumental skills while also showcasing more of Peter's guitar skills (also a great rhythmatist). (17.75/20)4. "Head" (18:36) impressive display of rhythmic expression and group unity--especially from Hellmut and Jan. Too bad about the somewhat cheesy riffs borrowed from British rockers like The Who. (35.5/40)5. "Sara auf der Gansewies" (2:01) bluesy cinema music using sax and guitar doubled up to present the plaintive main melody and bass. I like it though it is nothing Earth-shatteringly innovative. (4.375/5)Total Time: 42:59A rock album that draws from a lot of diverse influences including a Krautrock foundation that is heavily steeped in Can-like Kosmische Musik, Steve Winwood organ-based Blues-Rock, The Who's new and more concise Rock 'n' Roll, Chicago Transit Authority jazz-rock, and many of the psychedelic influences that tap into (or arise from) Middle Eastern and Oriental influences. It is also obvious that the band had heard Can, King Crimson, Brainbox/Focus, The Who, and The Mahavishnu Orchestra. Despite their jazzification of a lot of their instrumental performances, the music here feels quite solidly founded in blues-rock structures and motifs--which makes them feel much more akin to bands like The Spencer Davis Group and Traffic. They may have been inspired by The Mahavishnu Orchestra but they sound to me much more like Ash Ra Tempel, Amon D��l II, and/or Can. And, yes: Hellmut Hattler is a GREAT bass player! (How 'bout bringing he and Can's Jaki Liebezeit together with Triumvirat's J�rgen Fritz and Jan Akkerman for a Teutonic super super-group!)B-/3.5 stars; a nice addition to any prog rocker's music collection--especially if s/he is interested in the early foundational music of Krautrock, European Heavy Metal, and/or psychedelic prog.

"Zion I" (3:27) despite the Afro-Jamaican roots being expressed here, there is a laid-back sophistication here that predicts the direction that the band WAR would be taking in a couple years. (8.875/10)A2. "One More" (3:04) more laid back Afro-Caribbean sounds that incorporate bagpipe-like sounding instrument into the mix (as a kind of background reinforcer of the main guitar melody during the "choruses"). Satisfying if not fully developed: more like a little warm-up jam or �tude. (8.75/10)A3. "Getting It Back" (4:17) a bit of the drama of The Undisputed Truth and Nina Simone present in both the music and vocal performance. The horns are little too unified, harmonized too synchronically, even though the sax gets to break free and solo a bit in the final minute. (8.6667/10)A4. "Listen" (4:39) another song whose foundation sounds like it's informed by the current trends in American Soul/R&B being by Stax and Motown bands like Ike & Tina Turner, The Staples Singers, and the new kids on the block, The Undisputed Truth. A little boring with its endlessly repeating bass and melody lines. (8.6667/10)A5. "Rickshaw" (5:53) a motif that feels as if it carries over some of the worldly amalgamations achieved at the end of the 1960s by film soundtrack composers like Henry Mancini (Blake Edwards films), Burt Bacharach, and even Eric Burdon's War ("Spill the Wine"). (8.875/10)B1. "Dove" (10:52) a psychedelic jazz-blues jam that sounds like it came straight from San Francisco (Love, Santana, even a little of The Doors) Really nice, satisfying SANTANA-like jam with great groove and lead guitar work from Patrick Patterson. (18.25/20)B2. "Bra" (5:03) more Stax Studios-like Soul/R&B music with a catchy lyric sung in choral chant style. Great bass, drums, rhythm guitar groove with perfect brass section arrangements. (9.125/10)B3. "The Message" (4:19) one of the band's more popular tunes--both as an anthem and as a concert crowd-pleaser. It's a little simple and rather monotonous but apparently the words have significance that draw people in. (8.75/10)B4. "Rastafarian Folk Song" (3:09) exhibiting as fact that not all Jamaican or Rastafarian music is or has to be registered/rendered as Reggae music. Well presented as both engaging music as well as educational fodder. (8.875/10)Total Time 44:43What I hear here is a band who feels that it is their mission to unify African and Caribbean musical traditions with the Soul and Rhythm & Blues of the United States--to open the minds of Anglo-Americans to the interracial trends toward blending and fusion that had been emerging with the 1960s Civil Rights Movement and Anti-War, anti-establishment, counter-cultural revolution.B/four stars; a nice collection of fairly simple Afro-Caribbean Soul/R&B that has two highlight songs. I'd consider this more proto-prog than straightforward prog, Jazz-Rock, or J-R Fusion.

items.body: Review by siLLy puPPy — One of the more unusual progressive bands to emerge from the 1970s boom in the Netherlands, HETPANDORRA ENSEMBLE existed from 1973 until 1980 and left one album in its wake and very little infoabout its existence with nobody even sure of where the band was formed exactly. This band that wasled by guitarist Dolf Planteijdt who eschewed the symphonic prog tendencies of fellow Dutch actslike Focus or even more pop-fueled vocal acts like Earth & Fire but rather the band featured abizarre mishmash of heavy King Crimson guitar angst, Mahavishnu Orchestra inspired jazz fusion andextreme free improvisation liberties with varying musical motifs suddenly shifting midstream intosomething completely different. In addition to the more contemporary prog references, this band wasalso smitten with the abstract modern classical styles of George Crumb as well as impressionistssuch as Ravel and Bartok's Eastern European folklore works.The ENSEMBLE's entire presentation itself was a little odd with this act featuring only five membersand releasing a single album ironically titled III in 1978. What makes it even weirder is that thecover looks like a Patti Smith reject which honestly conveys absolutely nothing about the musicinside. No wonder this talented band was overlooked and lost to the annals of time! The lineup onIII features the cast members of Planteijdt (guitars), Dolf Planteijdt (guitars), Roland Brunt(flute), Gert-Jan Blom (bass) and Wilfred Snellens who replaced the recently deceased Jean Eble. Thealbum was released on the Disaster Electronics label and originally featured five tracks however the2012 Modulus reissue adds an extra seven bonus tracks of unreleased material.For all its eclecticism, HET PANDORRA ENSEMBLE was primarily steeped in complex jazz fusion motifsthat incorporated angular avant-prog complexities and King Crimson's "Red" as a template for gnarledguitar tones. The album displays a fairly interesting balance between skronky dissonance and morecleverly constructed melodic touches implementing everything from moments of space rock to Spanishflamenco. Three tracks "Door Mekaar," "Kanon Pittoresk" and "Karotten" all extend past the 10-minuteplaying time while the remaining two are much shorter clocking in under 5. "Kanon Pittoresk" is theperfect example of this band's extremities meandering from super chill to ridiculously sped uptempos and sizzling guitar soloing with a rather Latin-inspired bass groove. The band's album iscompletely instrumental with no vocals except a very a single moment of wordless chanting."Door Mekaar" showcases a reimagined King Crimson take on jazz fusion with twin guitar attacks andover-the-top complex arrangements while "Kanon Pittoresk" is more of a wild free-for-all that deftlyblends angular avant-prog fusion with more melodic rock hybridizations. The short track "Ritme 7000"serves only as a palette cleanser. It has sort of a medieval folk feel but only distantly. "Drei"takes a complete 180 and introduces a chamber rock style with a lengthy shrill monotone that slowlygenerates a creepy mood setting that pretty much stays in droning mode for 4 1/2 minutes with only afew surprise vocal chants and occasional tinkling of random sounds. "Karotten" ends the album withcontinues the detached eeriness of its predecessor and slowly transmogrifies into a guitar drivenseries of KC inspired works that evolve into a more fiery example of jazz fusion thus taking thealbum full circle. HET PANDORRA ENSEMBLE was sort of the fish out of water and even though it joined the ranks of theprog universe late in the game still retained that fiery experimental passion that exploded in thelate 1960s and became somewhat commercialized by 1973. III is a rather unpredictable slice of Dutchprog that sounds like no other. A second album was in the works but never came to fruition leaving aslew of musical carcasses to gather dust on the shelves for many decades before finally emerging asa whopping double album reissue in 2012. While the album could use some fine-tuning to make it morecohesive and sometimes feels extremely disjointed, for those with an appetite for wild untamedartistry run amok then this one will prove quite satisfying.

items.body: Review by Heart of the Matter — This fantastic concert, advertised as the "solo albums tour" in order to capitalize the expectatives originated in their 1975 sabatical, dedicated by each band member to their own project, remained until its 50th anniversary as a legendary, sought-after bootleg. Now officially released, it presents us with a Yes formation, including Patrick Moraz on keyboards (Wakeman's replacement), shining in the full splendour of their mid-seventies. Bold, exploratory and going full throttle from the start, the band is up to the energy level displayed in their previous studio release, the album Relayer. This is well represented here, of course, by Sound Chaser and the side-long epic The Gates of Delirium. Also, the same virtuosism and powerful sonic brilliance are put into the staple versions, such as Siberian Kathru and I've Seen All Good People, and an extraordinary rendition of Ritual, sending sparks from the bottom of those Topographic Oceans.The songs coming from the solo albums, in the form of excerpts taken from Jon Anderson's Olias Of Sunhillow and Moraz' Story Of I, offer a welcome relaxing moment, including also a newly fashioned, acoustic rendition of Long Distance Runaround, so brief as full of charm.What else? Oh, yeah, all this comes from the hearts and hands of musicians listening to each other tight, instead of to a metronome. Better to seize than to miss, don't you think?

items.body: Review by BrufordFreak — A second studio album put together in 1971 in London under the supervision of producer Tony Visconti (and also receiving the artistic talents of Roger Dean for the album art).1. "Beautiful Seven" (6:45) some soulful High Life music that has the advantage of Western rock production values to bring about better definition to and performances from each of the individual instruments. (Tony is figuring out how to mic and engineer this band!) The melodies, engineering, and mixes here are so much more superior to anything on the band's previous album (which was released within the same calendar year). The SANTANA-like jam that emerges in the final minute is what I've been looking more for. Still, the overall quality of the sound and performances is so much better than Osibisa. (13.75/15)2. "Y Sharp" (6:21) Memphis Blues-Rock sounding like it's coming straight out of the Stax recording studios--as if Isaac Hayes and David Porter were composing their music! Very enjoyable, nicely-polished mostly-instrumental music of a generic type that the musicians are embellishing with satisfactory spirit and inspiration. (9.125/10) 3. "Spirits Up Above" (7:18) a song that opens up sounding like PROCOL HARUM or THE SPENCER DAVIS GROUP setting up a ballad. But then the unusual tandem of trumpet and flute present the dirge-like melody lines over wah-wah-ed electric guitar and baritone sax. Wow! This is then trumped by the entrance and vocal presence of a church-like "Baptist" choir singing what could be a eulogy for a minute or so. Then the band suddenly kicks into Blues-Rock third gear with a two-chord vamp over which Robert Bailey's electric piano solos over Roy Bedeau and Sol Amarfino's excellent bass and drumming, respectively. Wendel Richardson's guitar solo is next and it's really cool with chord sliding and multi-note picking, all the while the horn section is supporting with its smooth long notes--until the seventh minute when the individual horns start to meander off onto their paths. What an awesome jam! This is by far the best thing I've heard from this band so far! (14.75/15)4. "Survival" (6:19) opening with some in-studio banter before Wendel (at least, I'm assuming it's Wendell) leading the band into a West African drum-and-chant opening (lasting 90 seconds!). I love this! And then at 1:45 the full band joins in, transitioning the music into some Memphis-ized High Life music--one that has some serious funk groovin' coming from Roy and Wendell as well as Robert's full organ chords and the tight horn section's accents and dominating lead melody blasts. In the middle of the fifth minute as Loughty Amao breaks free to solo with his tenor sax the rest of the band breaks into What's Going On-like party mingling noise in the background. Another awesome song! (9.5/10)5. "Move On" (4:34) opening with the "Oh-See-Bee-Sah" chant, the bass and percussion soon jump in with Wendel strumming acoustic guitar in a Django fashion to create a Caribbean-sounding High Life motif over which Wendel sings in a forceful Eric Burdon or Terry Kath-like singing voice and style, which changes the feel of the music into something more akin to War-like Jazz-Rock. Interesting. I like the sound palette, stylistic variety, but overall something's not quite working (besides the slightly murky overall mix). Maybe it's a bit over-filled: too busy; the Rock elements feel a little under-prepared and forced. (8.75/10)6. "Rabiatu" (5:07) a nice African-familiar High Life motif is taken into bluesier territory by all of the electrified instruments: Hammond organ, electric guitar, and watered-down bass line. The percussion line interlude in the third minute is cool--especially with Wendel's percussive rhythm guitar muted strumming and the deep, distant bass lines coming from both Ray's bass and Robert's Hammond. The horn work is very effective--very adeptly arranged. (8.875/10)7. "Woyaya" (4:27) PROCOL HARUM-like Hammond organ chords open this one before Wendel (barely) joins in to start the vocal choir up with his single-voiced recitation of the main lyric and melody, which is thereafter picked up by the whole band as a choir. They sound a bit like they're ending their night in an Irish pub with a drunken sing-a-long of some national (or local) anthem. Once they reach the fourth minute, as the choir join in singing the song title work over and over, things feel quite tight, but then they break into a percussion-only jam to finish it off for the final 45 seconds. Too bad! That "Woyaya" chant could've gone on a bit longer. A cool song--that could very easily be made into a whole-crowd anthem--that feels, to my mind, to be too loosely thrown together and condensed almost unnaturally when it could've been a nice eight or nine minute song. (8.875/10)Total Time: 40:44What a great leap forward for this band! Tony Visconti has figured the band out (proving his genius) and gotten superior sound, spirited performances of inspired compositions from this talented ensemble.A-/five stars; a minor masterpiece of mostly very-well-produced, very well composed African Jazz Rock. Very highly recommended.

items.body: Review by BrufordFreak — A newly-formed band of West African-born musicians get together in a London studio to try to create music for a studio album. The sessions had the support of up-and-coming producer Tony Visconti (The Move, Procol Harum, T. Rex, David Bowie, Magna Carta, Gentle Giant, Strawbs) and the album cover the art work of the one and only Roger Dean! Osibisa was released by MCA Records in June of 1971.1. "Dawn" (7:03) built over a two-chord bass and guitar vamp, the horns and percussion section start out rather tamely while Teddy Osei vocalizes in West African fashion beneath the soloing instruments (Hammond organ, electric guitar, flute, ). Of all the soloists only the first, Robert Bailey's Hammond organ, feels truly inspired, the rest feel as if they're just going through the motions of a song they've played a million times and feel bored performing in the relatively-unresponsive confines of a studio. (I'm suggesting that this song probably goes over bigger in a live concert setting.) (13/15)2. "Music for Gong Gong" (5:29) presenting a sound that feels more Caribbean-familiar, the horns feel quite engaged as does Robert Bailey's organ (once again). The rest of the band feels as if they're moving through rudiments, coming off a previous night's bender with some sluggishness and, perhaps, a slight hangover. The two two-chord vamp progressions lack the inspired embellishments that, say, a Santana or Mandrill might add. The highly-touted percussionists finally start to show some life (and spirit) in the second half of the fourth minute (when the rest of the instruments back out). (8.75/10)3. "Ayiko Bia" (7:53) from the very opening call-and-response chants this one feels fully-engaged, fully-representative of African High Life music. The rhythm section is next to expose their shtick before the horns add a kind of Memphis Horns layer. Then the organ-based music breaks open a different, softer approach to the opening's call-and-response, making this the main motif for the song to build itself around. At 2:40 the organ swirls and the horns activate as we enter an instrumental section for some guitar soloing from Wendel Richardson. So far, Robert Bailey is really the only instrumentalist in the band that really impresses me: the dude is so engaged and so creative. Mac Tontoh gets the next solo with his trumpet as the response choir activates as if the trumpet is now their call master. Then, around 5:30 we get another break from textural instruments so that the percussionists can have a party. I like these sections (but then I'm a sucker for all percussion polyrhythmic weaves). (13.375/15)4. "Akwaaba" (4:20) borrowing from American New Orleans blues-jazz the band establishes a weave that feels similar to the previous song in terms of the instrumentation populating it but the mood and vibe feels quite different: much more Americanized. Even the melody lines used by the horns, organ, and lead guitar are far more similar to the fare coming out of Western/American blues artists. A little too bland and studio suppressed to excite me. At the end of the song the four chord progression is repeated over and over with the vocal choir shouting out the letter-by-letter spelling of the band's name before the horn sections group blasts finish things off. (8.75/10)5. "Oranges" (4:40) another song that feels quite founded in American blues music (like Wilson Pickett)--until 1:15 when trumpeter Mac Tontoh is set up for a solo (over some more-circumscribed Wilson Pickett-like drum-and-bass music). The choir joins in, sometimes working in two groups (or two tracks) repeating the song name over and over before a brief sax bridge unveils a thinned out passage over which Wendell lays down a solid Southern Blues-Rock guitar solo. Robert's electric piano work in the mid-range is quite interesting. (8.75/10)6. "Phallus C" (7:14) "fallacy" is really what they're saying as they put together a fairly simple High Life blues root over which the vocalists call-and-response approach tells the story of being misjudged according to stereotypes. The work of the horn players, especially Loughty Amao's baritone sax, as well as Robert's under-volumed Hammond and Wendell's aggressive Rock electric guitar, are all notable and respectable. I only wish the overall result were a little better. (13.375/15)7. "Think About the People" (4:21) starting out quite quietly as bass, percussionists, organ, and guitar all seem to be finishing their tuning and warm ups. Nearly a minute into the recording does anything congeal into forward motion. What results is a CURTIS MAYFIELD-like High Life tune with more social-consciousness lyrics about the need for revolution. At 2:25 the music segues into a brief kind of crescendo-acting motif (which may or may not be meant as a chorus) before the band returns to a pepped up version of the Curtis motif before disintegrating into . . . lights out. Time to go! (8.75/10)Total Time: 41:36Overall I have to say that this well-regarded band's debut studio album is highly underwhelming. I perceive that these songs may receive quite an injection of adrenaline (and enthusiasm) when performed in front of a live audience but they need to do something to get that actively-engaged spirit to come through in these studio recordings! (Is producer Tony Visconti to blame? Was the band's unusual instrumental palette too new for him?)C-/2.5 stars; a collection of sadly disappointing music that seems to lack inspiration and/or full engagement. For collectors only.

items.body: Review by Matti — (Revisiting my Colossus reviews from 2013, pt. 4)At the time of receiving this CD I simultaneously got one that introduced me to the New York based prog band IZZ, a member of which John Galgano has always been. What surprises me now, 13 years later, is that this has remained his sole solo album, and without a single review! In my brief original review I even speculated if this young-looking guy could become one of the most promising solo artists in the American prog scene. Well, that didn't happen. John Galgano's main instrument in the multi-vocal group IZZ is the bass. Here he plays also guitars and some keyboards. Two of the shorter songs he co-wrote with his wife and IZZ colleague Laura Meade whose vocals are heard on most tracks. This feature increases the obvious similarities to IZZ. There are however less keyboards, and perhaps several pieces have a more intimate atmosphere and less of the rollercoaster prog eclectism. Overall it's easy to hear this is American prog, with kindred spirit to the likes of Spock's Beard and Glass Hammer. Lots of vocal harmonies and a sharp production. The album deals with the tough question of being human in modern times. The brief, small-scale opener has only John's vocals and acoustic guitar. The five norm-length songs operate between pop accessibility and a little prog complexity in rhythmic structures and sonic colours. The heavily repetitive chorus on 'Bigger on the Inside' is less elegant than the rest of the song. 'Lucky for Me' is entirely sung by Laura, nice. 'This Is How It Happens' is an emotional highlight in its somber intimacy. I don't like the alienating way how Laura's vocals are treated on 'The Only Thing' but there are interesting details in the arrangement, as well as on the more energetic 'Look Around'.'1000' is a 19-minute, multi-part epic with a higher degree of eclectic variety and dynamics. While Galgano respects the 70's rooted symphonic prog tradition, his music always sounds contemporary 21st century prog rock. The guitar sound on some movements owes especially to Steve Howe. Again the vocals are treated here and there. The album's official outro is a Pt. 2 of the title track, but after that comes a hidden track, a beautiful but disappointingly short a cappella piece revisiting the song 'This Is How It Happens'. This is a fine album which definitely should have gained more attention. Four stars, although I wish there were more notable instrumentally oriented sections throughout the album, not only in the epic.

items.body: Review by A Crimson Mellotron — Released in 2003 on Music for Nations, 'A Natural Disaster' is the seventh studio album fromAnathema, and the first one written almost entirely by guitarist Daniel Cavanagh. Undeniably adarker offering, this album has always been the odd one out - neither a continuation of the band'ssmoldering death-doom early style, not a clear indicator of what future releases would sound like.Combining drab alternative rock tropes with atmospheric passages and acoustic interludes, 'A NaturalDisaster' is more of an attempt to redefine the purpose of the band. Sprinkled all over this albumare a myriad of great ideas, that are unfortunately way too scattered in the final mix, which makesthe album somewhat of a forgettable and unimpressive listen. The sorrowful music played on manytracks appearing here reminds me of Katatonia and Porcupine Tree, and more remotely of Paradise Lostand Riverside, which renders this particular Anathema album slightly derivative.Interestingly enough, featured on this album is Vincent Cavanagh's twin brother Jamie, who plays thebass guitar for the first time on a major release with the band, following his early departure fromthe original lineup of Anathema, sometime around 1990-91. And so, as an album I have been fairlycritical of, I have to say that there are fine moments that make up for the weaker parts. Suchinstances of inspired and original music include opener 'Harmonium' with its desperate tones andclaustrophobic atmosphere, the peculiar piece 'Balance', on which Vincent Cavangh sings through avocoder, creating a feel of coldness and distance that is backed up by the moody keyboards. The song'Pulled Under at 2000 Metres a Second' has a post-punk appeal and is one of the surprising entrieson 'A Natural Disaster', while the hauntingly serene title track sees female vocalist Lee Douglasproviding excellent guest vocals. The final 10-minute-long instrumental 'Violence' could have beenmore appropriately constructed in order to fit the aesthetics of the album, at least in my humbleopinion, while the rest of the songs don't do much for me. This album probably suffers from a lackof direction and coherence, but I understand that people find within it a sincere expression ofgrief and melancholy, which I am able to appreciate.

items.body: Review by Matti — (Revisiting my Colossus reviews from 2013, pt. 3)The organ loaded proto proggers The Gods were Ken Hensley's group before Uriah Heep. Due to the quickly changing line-up The Gods also makes references to King Crimson (Greg Lake) and Jethro Tull (John Glascock plays the bass on this album), and even to the Rolling Stones. I bet quite a many second-hand vinyl store customer has at first, for a second, wondered if "Genesis" contains early stuff of Peter Gabriel, Tony Banks and co. The listening experience is pretty ambivalent nevertheless.Energetic early heavy rock with plenty of vocal harmonies, all right! But before long all that, spiced up by psychedelic inter-speeches, is bursting out from the other ear. Hensley's, or the whole quartet's, skills at songwriting frankly weren't very mature yet. Esoteric's 2-CD reissue contains both stereo and mono version of the album plus four rather weak single tracks.

items.body: Review by Matti — (Revisiting my brief reviews written in Finnish for Colossus prog magazine in 2013, pt. 2)On their 8th album the French group Nemo continues on the heavy prog path. The opening track of this 2-CD features intriguing a cappella vocals in the style of Gentle Giant, and there will come some more GG-reminding hooks later. The blues rocking guitar work, in addition to metallic connotations, brings to mind GG's Gary Green. Interesting rhythmic details are hidden amidst heavy riffs. Surely there are also modern prog metal elements too, in the highly strung guitar soli and in the synth sequences.But above all Nemo's compositions are mostly clever and alluring. Within the two discs there obviously are less worthy pieces too, so with some editings this would have been stronger as a single CD. Nevertheless Nemo is a refreshing acquaintance, even for an anti-metal listener like me.

items.body: Review by Fercandio46 — Lito Epumer's career was an evolution that took him from progressive rock to jazz-rock fusion; his forays into folk music and his time learning from masters like Luis Alberto Spinetta led to a solo career where he emerged as a mature artist with a clear musical vision. Pasaje La Blanqueada, his second album, captures all his artistic interests, spanning both electric and acoustic styles, and showcases his virtuosity; for instance, the influence of Weather Report can be traced in the track "A.J.A.""El Betinez" features a modern drum rhythm and a guest appearance by Spinetta, who contributes scat vocals and guitar work. Subtle details lend the track an American feel while simultaneously imbuing it with an almost Eastern mysticism. The renowned bassist Guillermo Vadal� and drummer Sebasti�n Peycer� bring a wealth of experience to the project."15 de Julio" also features Spinetta, while "Dos Zorros" showcases Lito's sister, Mar�a Gabriela, a musician known for her work with Charly Garc�a as well as her own solo career, on acoustic guitar. The song takes its title from the fact that the two of them are the only ones playing guitar; it is a beautiful, simple, and deeply moving track that remains a poignant memory, given that she would pass away at a very young age in 2003."Zapatito" is an acoustic jazz piece where, accompanied by drums, the guitar plays atonally, reminiscent of Baden Powell, creating a powerful melody that fuses the musical styles of northern Argentina and southern Brazil, before morphing into Candombe, complete with the bandone�n."Turi Turi" is practically a new standard; the electric guitar roars, backed by a driving bass and drum rhythm section, while Lito plays with the speed of Pat Metheny or Allan Holdsworth, yet always with deep feeling.Following in the tradition of Argentine guitarists like Rodolfo Alchourr�n, he was able to capture a jazz feel as well as more intimate, personal modos, evoking the countryside or a special corner for self-reflection. Here, he performs an acoustic guitar duet with Armando Alonso, with whom he would go on to record an entire album years later.Guitar duets also feature on Wayne, but with a fusion twist, incorporating the keyboards of Juan Carlos "Mono" Fontana (Spinetta's keyboardist). He sets the stage for the title track, "Pje. La Blanqueada," where the unfolding arrangement gives way to various solos, keyboard, bass, and guitar taking turns, creating variations that effectively present three versions of the same theme within a single track."Silvia's Blues" is, as the title suggests, a blues, but a very special one; it is a tour de force that begins slow and languid before floating into a space-jazz-rock vibe, with the spirit of Don Cherry's trumpet evoked through Fontana's keyboards. Then there is Lito's powerful guitar, an instrument that seems to speak and tell stories. He is a guitarist well worth discovering, with plenty to say and even more to play.

items.body: Review by Fercandio46 — Miaou's second album is titled Make These Things Alright; for it, they doubled down on their fusion of sequenced tracks and live instrumentation, mixing the two in the studio in the style of Saint Etienne, who were also a trio.On "Future Pavilion," Tatsuki Hamasaki's guitar enters the mix; combined with Hiromi Hasegawa's drum groove, playing over Mayumi Hasegawa's cloud of synthesizers feels like performing somewhere it never rains, close to the sun.In *A Bird In The Hand*, they opt for a pattern of repetition and counterpoint; however, while their starting point is reminiscent of Stereolab, the extended melodic development, which always sounds alternative and modern, subsequently leads them toward the East. It is esoteric and provocative, even in its calmness."Silent Picture" unfolds in a near-psychedelic manner, reminiscent of Air, whereas "Tiger Note" is more energetic, shifting into a sound akin to The Breeders, complete with distortion."On A Sunday," by contrast, achieves an almost dreamlike, progressive atmosphere, evoking the ballads King Crimson crafted in the early 90s. The guitarist conjures a special aura with his notes, elevating the entirety of "Make These Things Alright" and bathing it in a radiant, rainbow-like glow. The premise of blending technology with indie rock had previously leaned too heavily toward Sonic Youth, but with "When Will You Come Home?", that fusion returned in all its glory, suspending time... and stopping the clocks in its wake.LASA reminded me of the Smashing Pumpkins, despite being instrumental, because that specific type of distortion, layered with something else underneath, is present in Miaou's sound; it acts as a bridge connecting the 90s to the early 2000s, eras that share so much in common, much like the tonal nuances offered by the trio.

items.body: Review by Fercandio46 — As Albert e L'uomo Nero begins, a host of sensations from the 1970s comes to mind, Giallo films, the opening of The Exorcist, the movies of Dario Argento, for L'Ombra Della Sera utilized original instruments from that decade to recreate that atmosphere as faithfully as possible. Yet, of course, that was merely the starting point; the true significance lies in the composition and execution using those instruments. In this regard, they succeed brilliantly, as the final result is far more than a mere exercise in nostalgia or a commercial imitation.The Mellotron gives way to the Minimoog on "Gamma," and the classical composition stirs the emotions without veering into melodrama, evoking the spirit of 1970s Italian cinema, rich in music and steeped in the mystery of mansions harboring dark family secrets. Progressive elements expand to take on the forms of jazz-rock and psychedelia; one hears echoes of Genesis, Camel, and even Klaus Schulze, all flowing together with complete naturalness.Ritratto di Donna Velata showcases the richness of a beautiful and delicate composition they are capable of, with the unusual vibraphone and Mellotron duet. Fantastic Fly, in the time of a classic Bolero, highlights the double keyboard ensemble of Agostino Macor and Alessandro Corvaglia, followed by Fabio Zuffanti's bass. From emotive to mysterious and then epic...leaving no corner unexplored, both internally and externally."Come Andromeda" is even more experimental and delves deeper into free jazz; in contrast, "La Traccia Verde" features a funk groove strongly driven by the interplay between keyboards and flute, reminiscent of the Brazilian-influenced side of Billy Cobham or Les McCann. They fit squarely within the Italian tradition of moving effortlessly between genres and making each one their own, shifting from progressive rock to jazz, much like Banco del Mutuo Soccorso, Alphataurus, and so many others."La Ballata Di Carini" is sung by Alessandro Corvaglia, accompanied by a harpsichord that creates an almost theatrical, operatic atmosphere; the instrumental section, featuring keyboards, bass, and drums?then takes flight, engaging in a dialogue with the piano and incorporating recorded spoken passages to craft a tribute to 1970s Italian film and televisi�n, a powerful decade when the likes of Ugo Tognazzi, Marcello Mastroianni, and Vittorio Gassman could command the screen simply by standing in front of the camera.Le Venti Giornate di Torino is dedicated to the television adaptation of Giorgio De Maria's 1977 novel of the same name, recreating that atmosphere of gothic terror in a nineteen-minute suite. With excellent scales that seamlessly transition between sections, despite its variety of rhythms, it evokes the energy and mystery of King Crimson and Yes, the drama and tension of Genesis, and the classical composers?and that ominous sense of decadence of the Romantic era.As "Cento Campane" arrives, we can already picture the masks of the Venetian Carnival... all of Italy is present, North and South, lost and mingling within that magical anonymity; a magic as potent as the enveloping keyboards and percussion. Then, seamlessly, the final track begins: "A Blue Shadow," featuring the poetic saxophone of Martin Grice, an elegy so timeless it sounds modern, casting a shadow within the light, much like candles that seem as though they will never go out.

items.body: Post-punk band False Flowers released an official visualizer for their cover of Adam and the Ants’ “Beat My Guest”. The song is the B-side to “Secret Futures”, a two-song single out now on Strange Club Records, with UK distribution through No Front Teeth Records. Guitarist Brian Hanover, who wrote lead track “Secret Futures”, described how the cover came together: “When we first started playing together in 2024 I mentioned wanting to cover this. The idea fell by the wayside until early Jan 2026, when I mentioned it again and by this point knew we could make this sound like us by adding atmosphere, moodiness, and a different energy; it needed to be done right to honor such a great song. By Feb 2026 we had recorded it for the B side of Secret Futures.” ‘Beat My Guest’ backs the ‘Secret Futures’ single “Secret Futures” b/w “Beat My Guest” is the follow-up to False Flowers’ self-titled debut mini-LP. Both songs were recorded by Patrick Hills at Earthtone, the studio behind releases by 7 Seconds, Tera Melos and King Woman. Lead track “Secret Futures” pairs an upbeat, punk-rooted composition with lyrics about time spent on insignificant distractions rather than meaningful moments in life. The single has been available since July 3 through Strange Club Records, with digital release also through Amazon and iTunes and streaming on Apple Music, Deezer and Tidal, among other platforms. A self-produced music video for “Secret Futures” launched July 10 on the band’s YouTube channel. The physical 7-inch vinyl is available to order through Strange Club Records. False Flowers is already working on a new album, planned for 2027. The band continues to play alongside acts including Home Front, Primitive Heads, MESS, Generacion Suicida, Alter Girl and Guilty Strangers, with two confirmed Sacramento, California shows: August 3, 2026 – Cafe Colonial, with Bleakness and Rose Lyon September 3, 2026 – Cafe Colonial, with Bloodstains, Máscaras and Riot Radio About False Flowers False Flowers is Lory Gil (also of Rad and Sick Burn) on keyboard and vocals, Brian Hanover (also of Hanover Saints, Whiskey Rebels and Union Hearts) on guitar and backing vocals, Conrad Melancon (also of Cold Trap and Mob Rule) on bass, and Craig Hancock (also of Rad and Sick Burn) on drums. The band’s dark, atmospheric post-punk draws comparisons to Siouxsie and the Banshees, Bauhaus, TSOL, The Damned and Christian Death. False Flowers debuted with a self-titled mini-LP before releasing the “Secret Futures” b/w “Beat My Guest” single on Strange Club Records, now backed by an official visualizer for the cover track.

items.body: Johannesburg gothic rock band The Awakening, led by Ashton Nyte, released the single and video “Until The Dawn” on 23 July 2026, the first material from the band’s upcoming 13th album, “The Lost Theatre”. The album is out 23 August 2026 through Intervention Arts. Nyte describes “Until The Dawn” as the track that started the new album: “[It] is the song that gave birth to The Lost Theatre. I’m always writing songs, but this one told me a new album was on the way, and it had to be the first single. It is essentially a song about the courage of asking for help. It is a song of hope.” The single is streaming on Spotify. ‘Until The Dawn’ opens The Awakening’s ‘The Lost Theatre’ “The Lost Theatre” is the follow-up to The Awakening’s 2024 self-titled album, which reached number 3 on Germany’s Deutsche Alternative Charts. All music and lyrics on the new album are written, composed and performed by Ashton Nyte, produced by Nyte at Intervention Studios in the US and published by Intervention Arts / ASCAP. The album and a selection of limited-edition items are available for pre-order through The Awakening’s stores in Germany, the UK and the US. The Lost Theatre Tour dates 2026 The Awakening will support the album with a run of German shows, following last year’s worldwide Haunting Tour, which included headline dates in Germany, Poland, France, the Netherlands, the US, Canada, the UK, Mexico and South Africa. Tickets are available through the band’s site. 2 September 2026 – Dortmund, Germany – Pauluskirche (solo) 3 September 2026 – Köln, Germany – Club Volta 4 September 2026 – Hamburg, Germany – Nochtspeicher 5 September 2026 – NCN Festival 6 September 2026 – Berlin, Germany – Maschinenhaus About The Awakening The Awakening is a gothic rock and darkwave band from Johannesburg, South Africa, built around singer, multi-instrumentalist and producer Ashton Nyte, who writes, records and produces the project’s material and also releases solo work and collaborations, among them recurring appearances with Beauty In Chaos. The band’s back catalogue includes the double album “The Passage Remains” (2022) and earlier releases such as “The Carriage” (2015), and it has toured Europe alongside Wayne Hussey of The Mission. The Awakening issued its self-titled album in 2024, previewed by the single “Mirror Midnight”, and returned in 2025 with the “Through The Veil” video and a European tour announcement. “Until The Dawn” now opens the band’s 13th album, “The Lost Theatre”, due 23 August 2026 and backed by a run of German tour dates in September.

items.body: Dark ambient/industrial act AMPS KILL released the EP “Avulse” on July 23, 2026. The instrumental release is available now on Bandcamp and Spotify, along with other major digital outlets. ‘Avulse’ traces the process of shedding the self “Avulse” has no lyrics. Its five track titles supply the emotional context for the music, which the project describes as exploring the removal of aspects of the self or of one’s life that block growth, in the way lizards, spiders and insects shed their skin to grow. The first four tracks, “Husk”, “Slough”, “Basilisk” and “Chronophage“, were released as standalone singles at the end of 2025. The closing track, “Des Pas Sur Les Cendres”, ties the EP together and draws its musical material from Claude Debussy’s piano piece “Des pas sur la neige”. Chronophage by Amps Kill AMPS KILL also released an official visualizer for “Chronophage”, viewable on YouTube. About AMPS KILL This project is the work of classically trained composer and improviser Stephen Bailey. A self-described “refugee of the classical music world,” Bailey completed his formal compositional training in 2015. Following the events of 2020, he found expression in extreme music and shifted his output toward the harsher, noise-oriented post-industrial sound of AMPS KILL, which he describes as focused on texture and intensity over melody and harmony, confronting the darkness of the post-pandemic world. The project released the album “Wretched Inheritance” on Bandcamp on July 25, 2024. “Avulse” is the project’s latest release, following the run of singles that make up its first four tracks.

items.body: A darkwave artist named Ella Rey has rapidly built an audience through the use of melancholic vocals, cold synthesizers, post-punk guitars and a carefully constructed gothic imagery. Her songs circulate on Spotify, YouTube, Shazam and social media. Yet almost nothing is publicly known about the person – or people – creating them. There are no interviews explaining Ella Rey’s background. No musicians are named. No producer discusses the recordings. No hometown, studio, label team or live history connects the digital identity to a conventional artist. But there is, however, one clear disclosure: Ella Rey uses artificial intelligence to create music and actually the whole project is as far as I am concerned AI from A to Z (albeit with human intervention in the direction of the songs and structure). Descriptions published on Ella Rey’s official YouTube channel state that AI forms part of the music-creation process. According to the disclaimer, AI tools support “generation and experimentation,” while a human directs, selects and refines the final results. The same wording accompanies numerous songs, including “Within,” “This Is How It Ends,” “Cold Blood Heart,” “Children of Night” and “The End of Always.” That disclosure clearly confirms that Ella Rey is an AI-assisted project. It does not reveal how much of each song comes from generative tools though and as far as we can gather it’s a lot, most probably 100% generation with some – clever – human intervention. The visual identity of Ella Rey is that of dark haired, attractive and emotionally distant female character, not that one of the usual performer. But also here it’s 100% AI (and those who experiment with AI images instantly will recognise the characteristics). At least one Instagram promotion for “Cold Blood Heart” explicitly labelled its imagery with the hashtag “#aiphoto.” A virtual artist but with a real audience If you thought that Ella Rey is just an obscure experiment buried on an anonymous channel, then think again. By July 2026, the project had reached roughly 110,000 monthly listeners on Spotify. Its most visible releases included “Cold Blood Heart,” “The Remnant,” “Within,” “Angels in Flames” and “Dancing with the Void.” The numbers show how quickly an unknown virtual artist can enter an established music scene. Unlike what you would expect for these kind of plays, and followers, Ella Rey does not need a touring history, record-store presence or a recognisable group of musicians to compete for attention. The project has a consistent identity, frequent releases (although some are clearly rushed to hard as the AI use is obvious and even annoying) and material that fits existing listener habits. Whereas the project openly admits that AI contributes to the music, the official disclaimer also claims that a human directs, selects and refines the results. Logical. A track like “Within” for instance is an excellent track, turn it the way you want it. And the 145k views are surely not all payola. I played it to a few colleagues who had never heard of the track and all agreed this was strong material. The other tracks are not all as strong and seem to be based too much on a structure used on “Within”. Musically Ella Rey sounds like Hante. and The Birthday Massacre filtered through Blutengel’s gothic melodrama, with occasional traces of Twin Tribes and Within Temptation. On “Within” we even discovered a vocal part that could well have been Erika Dunham of Unter Null. The volume of releases raises immediate questions Ella Rey’s catalogue grew at a pace that would demand intense work from a conventional band. During 2026, 35 (!!) new tracks appeared that mix darkwave, post-punk, synthpop, industrial metal, cinematic rock, gothic rock and symphonic metal. Genre movement in itself is not proof of automation of course, but 35 tracks clearly is a big tell-tale sign that something is off to start with compared to a normal music production flow. On the Ella Rey YouTube Channel (20.4k subscribers!!) you will find even more content, 62 videos. Note that the YouTube Channel also holds blogposts where the Ella Rey persona is posting updates like the below one (one one which real people actually respond as well): Ella Rey blogpost on YouTube What’s next for Ella Rey? An artist such as Ella Rey can remain on Spotify, Apple Music and YouTube Music, provided the distributor accepts the material, the operator controls the required rights and the project does not impersonate another artist or manipulate streams. The same catalogue would face larger obstacles elsewhere: Bandcamp: high probable rejection if the music is substantially AI-generated. CD Baby: due to their AI ban the platform cannot be used as the distributor. Deezer: likely AI labelling and exclusion from recommendations. TuneCore: the operator would need to establish that the generator used licensed training material. LANDR: restricted release volume and reduced store coverage. SoundCloud distribution: generators such as Suno would not qualify. The industry’s emerging position is not really banning AI music as such though, but it wants creators to disclose AI use, and make sure they control the rights, where others cannot clone real artists, or flood the catalogues. The same goes for manipulating streams, although a lot of bands and labels are guilty as hell here as well. The egos you know… Clear is that fully AI-generated virtual artists remain permitted on several major services, but they increasingly receive labels (with a lot of false alarms as well as we noticed in the past few months), reduced discovery, distributor restrictions and closer fraud monitoring. AI is a revenue model for Spotify Approximately 44% of all newly uploaded music (!!) on streaming platforms is AI-generated, but Spotify has recently removed over 75 million “spammy” AI tracks to combat royalty fraud. Officially, Spotify commissions zero AI tracks, though investigations have revealed an internal “Perfect Fit Content“ program that relies heavily on thousands of tracks from “fake artists”. Spotify partners with specific production companies or session musicians to create thousands of low-cost, functional background tracks (e.g., lo-fi, chill piano, ambient noise) under hundreds of fake pseudonyms. Spotify then aggressively pushes these “artists” into its most popular owned-and-operated mood playlists (like Deep Focus or Chill Lofi Study Beats). Because these tracks are accepted under a much lower royalty rate, Spotify keeps a larger share of the subscription pool. While these “ghost tracks” traditionally relied on human session musicians writing thousands of songs under fake names, the industry consensus is that these production houses are rapidly shifting to AI generation tools to lower costs even further.

items.body: California-based experimental extreme metal duo Antania has joined the roster of Italian label Argonauta Records, the band and label confirmed. The move follows Antania’s earlier deal with Triad Records, which released the duo’s second album, “The God Complex,” in January 2024. The band builds its sound without guitars or bass, using synthesizers, distortion and electronic manipulation instead. The duo, made up of Dr. Luna and Kali Mortem, mixes industrial black metal with experimental electronics, combining mechanical rhythm programming, low-end bass tones and dense atmospheric production. The band cites Dodheimsgard, Mysticum and Thorns among its extreme-metal influences, alongside the industrial electronics of Skinny Puppy and Ministry. Grand Sounds PR, the agency handling the announcement, describes Antania’s music as “an oppressive fusion of mechanical precision, crushing low-end frequencies and bleak, immersive atmospheres.” Lyrically, Antania draws on true crime, psychological horror and real-world violence, a focus already present on “Lividity” and continued through “The God Complex.” Antania joins Argonauta Records roster No debut release through Argonauta Records has been announced yet; the label and band have said only that more details will follow in the coming weeks. Argonauta Records, founded in Genoa, Italy in 2012 by Gero Lucisano, has built a roster centered on doom, sludge, stoner and extreme metal acts, including Los Natas, Mitochondrial Sun, Ancient VVisdom and Snail. About Antania Antania is a two-piece project from Joshua Tree, California, formed by Dr. Luna and vocalist Kali Mortem, who is a U.S. Army veteran and was featured in Jeremy Saffer’s book “Daughters of Darkness.” The duo released its debut album, Lividity, in June 2023, a bass-heavy record with songs drawn from true-crime accounts of murder and violence. Antania then signed with Triad Records in December 2023, and the label released the duo’s follow-up album, “The God Complex,” on January 5, 2024. In 2024, the band toured Europe alongside Psyclon Nine and Devil M. The band now moves to Argonauta Records for its next chapter, with a debut release for the label expected to be detailed in the coming weeks.
